name: Grade 8
theme: The Church through history, and preparing for Confirmation

lessons.title: Jesus founds the Church
lessons.idea: Jesus founded one Church on Peter and the apostles. At Caesarea Philippi Peter confessed him as the Christ, and Jesus gave him the keys of the kingdom. That office continues in the Pope and the bishops.
lessons.question: Why Peter?
lessons.activity: “Keys and rock” study (30 min). Annotate Matthew 16:13–19 with Isaiah 22:20–22 (the royal steward’s key) and John 21:15–17 (“Feed my sheep”). Students record what authority Jesus gives and how the apostolic office continues (bishops as successors, Pope as successor of Peter).
teach: Jesus founded the Church by preaching the Kingdom, choosing the Twelve and giving Peter a unique role (CCC 551–553, 765). The Church was “born” from the pierced side of Christ and manifested at Pentecost (CCC 766).
The keys signify authority to bind and loose (Matthew 16:19; Isaiah 22). The same power is shared with the apostles (Matthew 18:18) and Peter is always first in the lists (CCC 552).
Apostolic succession passes the apostles’ mission to bishops through laying on of hands (CCC 861–862). The Pope, as Peter’s successor, is the visible principle of unity (CCC 882).
Early witnesses such as Clement of Rome (c. 96) and Irenaeus (c. 180) point to Rome’s special authority. Present these respectfully.
talk: How do we see succession today?
quiz: Jesus built his Church on…|Peter|Paul|Judas|Herod|0|Matthew 16:18.
The keys signify…|Locks|Authority|Silence|Wealth|1|Isaiah 22:22.
Peter’s successor is…|The king|The prior|The emperor|The Pope|3|CCC 882.
lessons.life: Learn the name of the Pope and the line of succession.
lessons.saint: Clement of Rome: the pope who wrote to Corinth and showed that the apostles’ authority was handed on.
misc: “Jesus never intended an institutional Church.”
“Peter was just the first among equals with no special role.”
lessons.mem: “You are Peter, and on this rock I will build my church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it.” (Matthew 16:18)
lessons.hook: Show a ring of keys and ask: “What does the person who holds the keys do?” Read Matthew 16:13–19 and note the question Jesus asks first: “Who do you say that I am?”
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain the keys, the rock and apostolic succession in a short paragraph.

script.open: Write on the board, “Whom did Jesus leave in charge?” Take answers. Then ask, “How do we know?”
teach: Read Matthew 16:13-19. Say: “At Caesarea Philippi, Jesus asked, ‘Who do you say that I am?’ Simon Peter answered, ‘You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.’ Jesus said, ‘Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jonah… you are Peter, and on this rock I will build my church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it. I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven, and whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven.’ Jesus gave Simon a new name, Rock (Cephas in Aramaic), and the keys, which in Isaiah 22 belonged to the king’s steward, the chief official. Peter has a special authority.”

Say: “Jesus also chose twelve apostles and gave them authority: ‘Whoever listens to you listens to me.’ (Luke 10:16) He sent them: ‘Go therefore and make disciples of all nations.’ (Matthew 28:19) After the Resurrection he gave them the power to forgive sins (John 20:23). He promised the Holy Spirit to lead them into all truth. And to Peter: ‘Feed my sheep.’ (John 21:17) The Church is not a human club but a community founded by Christ on the apostles, with Peter at the head.”

Say: “The apostles had to hand on their ministry. In Acts 1, Matthias replaced Judas. Paul named Timothy and Titus to appoint elders. This is called apostolic succession: the bishops are the successors of the apostles, and the bishop of Rome, the Pope, is the successor of Peter. St. Clement’s letter shows this was understood in the first century. The Catholic Church is the one that can trace its bishops back, in an unbroken line, to the apostles. This gives us confidence that the teaching is the teaching handed on by Christ.”
ask: What did Jesus give Peter? (A new name, the keys, authority to bind and loose.)
What is apostolic succession? (Bishops succeeding the apostles in an unbroken line.)
Who is Peter’s successor today? (The Pope, the bishop of Rome.)
practice: Draw a vertical chain: Jesus, Peter and the apostles, their successors, the bishops today.
Mark the key Bible verses beside each link (Matthew 16:18; Luke 10:16; John 21:17; 2 Timothy 2:2).
Add the name of your own bishop and the current Pope at the bottom.
Explain the chain to a partner.
script.close: Pray for the Pope and your bishop. Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Find out the name of your bishop.”

tryit: Trace the line from Jesus to the apostles to their successors.
Mark where Peter appears.
Say what the keys mean.
lessons.saintStory:
Clement was the fourth bishop of Rome, about AD 88 to 97, after Peter, Linus and Cletus. Around the year 96, the Christians in Corinth removed some of their appointed leaders, and the community split. Clement wrote them a letter on behalf of the Church in Rome, which is the oldest Christian writing outside the New Testament.
In it, he wrote that the apostles had appointed bishops and deacons, and had arranged for others to succeed them when they died, so that the order would continue. He urged the Corinthians to restore peace and humility. “Why are there strife and anger and division among you?” Remarkably, the bishop of Rome intervened in a church far away, and it was received with respect. The letter was read in Corinth at Mass for generations.
Tradition says Clement was exiled to the Crimea, and martyred. He is named in the Roman Canon of the Mass.

lessons.title: The Church as mystery, sacrament, body
lessons.idea: The Church is a mystery that cannot be exhausted by one image. She is the sacrament of salvation, the Body of Christ, the People of God, the Temple of the Spirit and the Bride of Christ. Each image shows something true.
lessons.question: Which image helps you?
lessons.activity: “Illustrate three images” (30 min). Students choose three images from CCC 753–757 (flock, vineyard, building, bride), read Ephesians 1:22–23 and 5:25–32, and make a poster that pairs a drawing with a short explanation and a verse.
teach: The Church is a “mystery” — a visible society and a spiritual reality (CCC 770–771). She is “the universal sacrament of salvation” (CCC 774–776).

The Body of Christ: Christ is the head, we are members (Ephesians 1:22–23; CCC 787–795). The People of God: a priestly, prophetic and royal people (CCC 781–786). The Temple of the Spirit (CCC 797–798).
The Bride of Christ (Ephesians 5:25–32): Christ loves and gives himself for her (CCC 796). This shows both tenderness and fidelity.
Vatican II (Lumen Gentium) uses these images. Acknowledge that the Church’s members are sinners (CCC 827).
talk: How is the Church both human and divine?
quiz: The Church is called the Body of…|Mary|Peter|Paul|Christ|3|CCC 779.
The Church is also the…|Servant of kings|Mother of all|Queen of earth|Bride of Christ|3|CCC 796.
Lumen Gentium is a…|Council of Trent|Encyclical of Leo XIII|Vatican II document|Hymn|2|CCC 748.
lessons.life: Read Lumen Gentium chapter 1.
lessons.saint: Catherine of Siena: a lay woman who loved the Church so much that she told the pope to come home.
misc: “The Church is just a human organization.”
“The Church is only the clergy.”
lessons.mem: “He has put all things under his feet and has made him the head over all things for the church, which is his body.” (Ephesians 1:22–23)
lessons.hook: Put students in groups and give each one an image (body, people, bride, temple). Ask: “What does this image say about our relationship to Christ and to each other?”
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain three images of the Church and what each teaches.

script.open: Draw a stick-figure body on the board and ask students to label the parts with jobs in a parish: hands, eyes, feet. Say, “What happens when one part stops working?” Use their answers to open Paul’s image.
teach: Say: “The Church is a mystery. That means she is not only a human organization, but a reality with a divine side that we cannot fully grasp. The Catechism says the Church is ‘visible and spiritual,’ a human community and the presence of Christ. Scripture gives us images of the Church. The People of God: God’s chosen people, now made up of all nations (1 Peter 2:9). The Body of Christ: Christ is the head and we are the members (1 Corinthians 12). The Temple of the Holy Spirit: ‘Do you not know that you are God’s temple?’ (1 Corinthians 3:16). The Bride of Christ: Christ loves her (Ephesians 5). The Flock: Christ is the Good Shepherd (John 10). The Vine and branches: ‘I am the vine, you are the branches.’ (John 15)”

Say: “The Church is also called a sacrament: ‘a sign and instrument of communion with God and of unity among all men.’ (Lumen Gentium 1) She is the visible sign through which Christ is present to the world and gives grace. She is not perfect. The Church is made up of sinners, and always needs reform. Catherine of Siena saw this, and loved the Church even more. The Church is called holy because Christ is holy, and because the Holy Spirit works in her, even though her members sin.”

Say: “Paul’s image of the Body is the most powerful. ‘Now you are the body of Christ and individually members of it.’ If you are baptized, you are a member. Each member has a role. When one suffers, all suffer. Christ lives in the Church; when Saul persecuted Christians, Jesus said, ‘Why do you persecute me?’ This is why we say the Church is not optional. To love Christ is to love his body. St. Cyprian said, ‘No one can have God for his Father who does not have the Church for his mother.’”
ask: Name three images of the Church. (People of God, Body of Christ, Temple of the Spirit, Bride, Flock.)
What does it mean that the Church is a sacrament? (A visible sign and instrument of God’s presence.)
How can the Church be holy and have sinners? (Christ is holy; the Spirit works in her.)
practice: Divide into groups. Each takes an image: People of God, Body of Christ, Temple of the Spirit, Bride, Flock, Vine.
Draw it, and write the Scripture verse and what it shows about the Church.
Present to the class.
End by writing: “Being a member of the Church means that I…”
script.close: Pray for the Church: “Lord, make your Church holy.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Ask an adult what they love about the Church.”

tryit: Match the images of the Church to Scripture.
Explain what each shows.
Draw one.
lessons.saintStory:
Catherine Benincasa was born in 1347 in Siena, Italy, the twenty-fourth of twenty-five children. At six or seven she had a vision of Christ, and decided to give her life to him. Her family wanted her to marry. She cut off her hair in protest, and finally they allowed her to become a lay Dominican, living at home in prayer.
She spent hours praying in a small room, and then began to nurse the sick, including plague victims and a man with leprosy. People were drawn to her. She started writing letters to everyone: popes, kings and ordinary people, all in a direct and loving voice. She did not know how to write, and dictated them at first.
At that time, the popes lived in Avignon, in France, rather than Rome. Catherine wrote to Pope Gregory XI, urging him to return. In 1377 he did. She also spent her last years trying to heal the Church from the Western Schism. She died in 1380, at thirty-three, and is a Doctor of the Church.

lessons.title: Marks of the Church
lessons.idea: The four marks of the Church — one, holy, catholic and apostolic — are named in the Nicene Creed. They are gifts of Christ and also tasks for believers. Each is real, though imperfectly lived.
lessons.question: How does each mark appear today?
lessons.activity: “Marks and evidence” (30 min). Students take each mark and give biblical grounds, historical evidence and a present-day example (one: Ephesians 4:4–6, the Mass worldwide; holy: saints; catholic: 1.3 billion on every continent; apostolic: unbroken lines of bishops). Debate: how do wounds to unity challenge the first mark?
teach: One: one Lord, one faith, one Baptism (CCC 813–822). Unity is a gift; divisions among Christians are a wound. The Church works for Christian unity (ecumenism, CCC 820–822).
Holy: because Christ sanctifies her through sacraments and the Spirit (CCC 823–829). The Church has saints in every age and sinners too.

Catholic: “according to the whole”: the fullness of faith and means of salvation, and sent to all people (CCC 830–856). Apostolic: founded on the apostles, teaching their doctrine and governed by their successors (CCC 857–865).
Teach respectfully about other Christians, who share Baptism and many truths (CCC 818–819).
talk: How does each mark show up?
quiz: Unity includes…|One language|One faith, worship, governance|One building|One culture|1|CCC 815.
Catholicity means…|Roman|Local|Fullness and universality|Large|2|CCC 830.
Apostolicity means…|Eastern|Quick|Founded on the apostles|Ancient|2|CCC 857.
lessons.life: Pray for unity among Christians.
lessons.saint: Ignatius of Antioch: the bishop who first used the words “Catholic Church” and was eaten by lions.
misc: “If the Church is holy, no one in it can be bad.”
“Catholic means ‘Roman’ and nothing more.”
lessons.mem: “There is one body and one Spirit… one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of us all.” (Ephesians 4:4–6)
lessons.hook: Ask: “How would you identify a particular school?” (name, uniform, motto). Introduce the marks as the Church’s identifying signs.
lessons.assess: Ask students to name the four marks, explain each and give one sign that it is real today.

script.open: Ask, “How would you tell a real $20 bill from a fake? What marks do you check?” Take answers. “How could we tell the real Church of Christ? The Creed gives four marks.”
teach: Say: “In the Nicene Creed, we say, ‘I believe in one, holy, catholic and apostolic Church.’ These are the four marks of the Church. One: the Church is one because her source is the Trinity, with one Lord, one faith, one Baptism (Ephesians 4:4-6). She is united in faith, sacraments and governance under the Pope and bishops. Christians are divided, and Jesus prayed ‘that they may all be one.’ (John 17:21) We work for unity, and pray for it.”

Say: “Holy: the Church is holy because Christ is holy, because he gave her the means of holiness (the sacraments, the Word) and because she produces saints. This does not mean that members are sinless. Catholic: the word means ‘universal’ or ‘according to the whole.’ She has the fullness of the faith and the means of salvation, and she is for all peoples, in all times and places. Apostolic: she is founded on the apostles, whose teaching she keeps, and whose authority is handed on through the bishops.”

Say: “These marks can be seen. There is one faith across the world: the same Creed, the same seven sacraments, the same Mass readings in every language. There is a Pope and bishops, tracing back to the apostles. There are saints in every age and country. Other Christian communities have real elements of truth and holiness, and we respect them; we do not say they have nothing. The Catholic Church teaches that the fullness of the means of salvation subsists in her. As Ignatius said, where Christ is, there is the Catholic Church.”
ask: Name the four marks. (One, holy, catholic, apostolic.)
What does ‘catholic’ mean? (Universal; the fullness of the faith for all.)
What do we do about divisions among Christians? (Pray and work for unity.)
practice: Make four columns: One, Holy, Catholic, Apostolic.
Under each, write a definition, a Bible verse, and one thing you can see in your own parish or diocese.
Add a test: What would a community lack if it were missing this mark?
Share with a partner.
script.close: Pray the Creed slowly, especially the line on the Church. Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Pray for Christian unity.”

tryit: Define each mark in a sentence.
Find a sign of each in your parish.
Test: could another community claim it?
lessons.saintStory:
Ignatius was bishop of Antioch in Syria around the year 100, probably a disciple of the apostle John. He was arrested during the reign of Trajan and sent as a prisoner to Rome to be killed by wild beasts. On the long journey, guarded by soldiers he called “ten leopards,” he wrote seven letters to churches along the way, and to Polycarp.
In them, he wrote about the unity of the Church around the bishop, “Where the bishop appears, there let the people be, just as where Christ Jesus is, there is the Catholic Church.” This is the earliest known use of the term “Catholic Church.” He also wrote of the Eucharist as “the medicine of immortality” and the flesh of our Savior Jesus Christ.
He begged the Christians in Rome not to rescue him: “I am the wheat of God, and I am ground by the teeth of wild beasts, that I may be found the pure bread of Christ.” He died in about 107.

lessons.title: Persecution and martyrs
lessons.idea: The first three centuries were years of persecution. Martyrs such as Stephen, Ignatius of Antioch, Polycarp, Perpetua and Felicity bore witness to Christ with their lives. “The blood of the martyrs is the seed of Christians.”
lessons.question: What is a witness?
lessons.activity: “Martyr profiles” (30 min). Groups read short excerpts from the Martyrdom of Polycarp and the Passion of Perpetua and Felicity, then make a profile card: who, when, charge, their words, what they teach us. Present, then discuss modern martyrdom today.
teach: The word “martyr” means “witness” (CCC 2473). Martyrdom is the supreme witness to the truth of faith (CCC 2473–2474). The Church honors martyrs as models and intercessors.
Ignatius of Antioch (c. 107) wrote on the way to Rome, “Let me be food for the wild beasts.” Polycarp (c. 155) refused to deny Christ: “Eighty-six years I have served him.”
Perpetua and Felicity (203) show young women’s courage. Tertullian wrote that “the blood of martyrs is the seed of Christians.”
More Christians died for the faith in the twentieth century than in all the previous centuries combined. Speak with sensitivity and hope.
quiz: Martyr means…|King|Priest|Warrior|Witness|3|CCC 2473.
Ignatius of Antioch was killed in…|Egypt|Greece|Spain|Rome|3|Tradition.
The blood of martyrs is the…|End of faith|Seed of Christians|Cost of war|Sign of defeat|1|Tertullian.
lessons.life: Pray for persecuted Christians.
lessons.saint: Perpetua and Felicity: two young mothers who died in the arena at Carthage in 203.
misc: “Martyrs wanted to die.”
“Persecution ended with Rome.”
lessons.mem: “Lord Jesus, receive my spirit… Lord, do not hold this sin against them.” (Acts 7:59–60)
lessons.hook: Read Acts 7:54–60 and ask what Stephen says as he dies. Note the echo of Jesus’ words from the Cross.
lessons.assess: Ask students to name two martyrs, what they said or did and what we learn from them.

script.open: Read aloud a short excerpt from the letters of Pliny to Trajan about Christians. Ask, “What did the governor find? What surprised him about these people?” Take notes on the board.
teach: Say: “For about three hundred years, Christians were persecuted by the Roman Empire. Nero blamed them for the fire in Rome in AD 64. Peter and Paul were killed. In AD 250, Emperor Decius ordered everyone to offer sacrifice to the Roman gods. Diocletian began the Great Persecution in 303, which was the worst. Christians were refused because they would not worship the emperor or the gods; because they met in secret; and because they were thought to be atheists, since they had no idols. Christians were arrested, tortured, put in arenas against wild beasts, burned or beheaded.”

Say: “The word ‘martyr’ means ‘witness.’ A martyr dies for the faith, because of hatred of Christ. The Church honors martyrs as having the greatest love (John 15:13). Stephen, killed in Acts 7, was the first. Ignatius of Antioch, Polycarp of Smyrna, Justin, Agnes, Lawrence, Cecilia, Perpetua and many others followed. Tertullian wrote, ‘The blood of the martyrs is the seed of the Church.’ The more the Church was persecuted, the more she grew, as people were impressed by the martyrs’ courage and joy.”

Say: “Not everyone was strong. Some, under torture, gave in, offering sacrifice or handing over the Scriptures. They were called the lapsed. After persecution ended, the Church debated how to treat them, and decided that they could return after penance. This is the origin of the sacrament of Reconciliation’s public penance. Christians also met in the catacombs, underground burial places in Rome, where they prayed, celebrated Mass over the tombs of the martyrs, and used symbols like the fish (ichthys) and the Chi-Rho. Today, there are still martyrs; in the 20th century there were more Christian martyrs than in all earlier centuries.”
ask: What does ‘martyr’ mean? (Witness.)
Why were Christians persecuted? (They refused to worship the emperor and the gods.)
What did Tertullian say about martyrs? (Their blood is the seed of the Church.)
practice: Read selections from Perpetua’s diary or the Martyrdom of Polycarp (a short excerpt).
In pairs, answer: What was she asked to do? What did she refuse? Why?
Write a short statement of what you would stand up for.
Share one.
script.close: Pray: “Holy martyrs, pray for us.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Pray for Christians who are persecuted today.”

tryit: Read a martyr’s own words.
Answer: what did she refuse, and why?
Say what the Church gained.
lessons.saintStory:
Vibia Perpetua was a noblewoman of about twenty-two in Carthage, in North Africa, with an infant son. Felicity was her slave, eight months pregnant. They were arrested in 203 with others for being Christian catechumens, under an order against conversion. Perpetua kept a diary in prison, one of the earliest writings by a Christian woman.
Her father, a pagan, begged her to offer incense and save herself. “Father, do you see this vessel? Can it be called by any other name than what it is?” “No.” “Neither can I call myself anything else than what I am, a Christian.” She and her companions were baptized in prison. Felicity gave birth to a daughter just days before, and a Christian woman adopted the baby.
On March 7, 203, they were sent into the arena. Wounded by a wild cow, Perpetua asked for a pin to fasten her torn tunic, out of modesty. They gave each other the kiss of peace, and were killed by the sword. Their names are in the Roman Canon.

lessons.title: Constantine and the councils
lessons.idea: In 313 Constantine ended the persecution of Christians. Soon the Church faced heresies, especially about who Christ is. Councils at Nicaea (325), Constantinople (381), Ephesus (431) and Chalcedon (451) defined the faith still professed in the Creed.
lessons.question: What did Nicaea teach?
lessons.activity: “Compare the creeds” (30 min). Place the Apostles’ Creed and the Nicene Creed side by side. Students highlight what Nicaea added (“begotten, not made, consubstantial with the Father”). Then match each council with the heresy it answered: Arianism, Macedonianism, Nestorianism, Monophysitism.
teach: The Edict of Milan (313) gave Christians freedom of worship. Constantine called the Council of Nicaea (325) to settle Arius’ claim that the Son was a creature. Nicaea taught that the Son is “consubstantial” (homoousios) with the Father (CCC 465, 242).
Constantinople (381) defended the divinity of the Holy Spirit and completed the Nicene Creed. Ephesus (431) called Mary Theotokos. Chalcedon (451) taught two natures in one Person (CCC 466–469).
The Church defines doctrine to protect the faith, not to invent it (CCC 88–90). The councils worked under the Spirit with the Pope’s authority.
Constantine’s patronage helped the Church but also brought entanglement with the state. Be honest about both sides.
quiz: Nicaea defined that the Son is…|Created|Lesser|A prophet|Consubstantial with the Father|3|CCC 465.
Arius taught that Jesus was…|A creature|Man only|God|Spirit|0|CCC 465.
The Nicene Creed is said at…|Weddings only|Sunday Mass|Funerals only|Baptism only|1|CCC 195.
lessons.life: Say the Nicene Creed with attention.
lessons.saint: Nicholas of Myra: a bishop who, tradition says, was at Nicaea and who gave in secret.
misc: “Constantine invented Christian doctrine at Nicaea.”
“Councils added new beliefs.”
lessons.mem: “We believe in one Lord, Jesus Christ, the only Son of God, … consubstantial with the Father.” (Nicene Creed)
lessons.hook: Ask: “Is Jesus a creature, or is he God?” Explain that the answer wasn’t obvious to everyone until the Church spoke clearly.
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain one council, the heresy it answered and the teaching it defined.

script.open: Display a coin or medal with Constantine’s image. Say, “The first Christian emperor. What would you ask him if he were alive?” Collect questions and see which ones the lesson answers.
teach: Say: “In 312, before a battle at the Milvian Bridge, Constantine saw a sign, the Chi-Rho, and the words ‘In this sign conquer.’ He won, and in 313, with Licinius, he issued the Edict of Milan, which gave Christians freedom of worship and returned their property. He later supported the Church with buildings, such as the Lateran basilica, and moved the capital to Constantinople. In 380, under Theodosius, Christianity became the official religion. Constantine was baptized on his deathbed in 337.”

Say: “With freedom came new challenges: how to be faithful when it was safe, and how to settle disputes about doctrine. Arius, a priest in Alexandria, taught that the Son was created, ‘there was a time when he was not.’ This would make Jesus less than God. To settle it, Constantine called the first ecumenical council at Nicaea in 325, with about 300 bishops. They declared that the Son is ‘begotten, not made, consubstantial with the Father.’ They wrote the first part of the Nicene Creed. Athanasius defended it for decades.”

Say: “Other councils followed. Constantinople I (381) defined the divinity of the Holy Spirit and completed the Creed. Ephesus (431) declared Mary Theotokos, Mother of God. Chalcedon (451) taught that Christ has two natures in one Person. These councils protected the faith about the Trinity and the Incarnation. The councils show how the Church works: bishops gather, with the Pope or his legates, to define the faith. The Holy Spirit guides the Church to preserve truth. We still pray their words in the Creed every Sunday.”
ask: What did the Edict of Milan do? (Gave Christians freedom of worship.)
What did Arius teach? (That the Son was a created being.)
What did Nicaea declare? (The Son is consubstantial with the Father.)
practice: Make a timeline with the four councils: Nicaea 325, Constantinople 381, Ephesus 431, Chalcedon 451.
Beside each, write the heresy and the Church’s answer.
Then find the matching line in the Nicene Creed.
Pray that line aloud.
script.close: Pray the Nicene Creed together. Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Look up the Nicene Creed and underline lines from Nicaea.”

tryit: Order the events from Milan to Nicaea.
Say what each Council added to the Creed.
Write the Creed line it defended.
lessons.saintStory:
Nicholas lived in the fourth century in Myra, in what is now Turkey. He was born into a wealthy family and orphaned young. According to old accounts, he used his inheritance to help the poor. In one story, he learned of a man who was too poor to give his three daughters a dowry, and who was about to sell them into slavery. In the night, Nicholas threw a bag of gold through the window, three times.
He became bishop of Myra, and was imprisoned during the persecution under Diocletian. Tradition says he attended the Council of Nicaea in 325, where he defended the faith against Arius. The same stories say that, passionately, he struck Arius. The more reliable fact is that Nicholas was known for charity and for protecting the poor and the falsely accused.
He died around 343. Stories of his gift-giving spread, and he became Santa Claus in many countries. He is patron of children and sailors.

lessons.title: The Fathers of the Church
lessons.idea: The Fathers of the Church are early teachers and bishops whose writings shaped doctrine and prayer. Ignatius, Justin, Irenaeus, Athanasius, Basil, Gregory, Chrysostom, Ambrose, Jerome and Augustine are among them.
lessons.question: Who are they?
lessons.activity: “Read a Father” (30 min). Provide short excerpts: Athanasius (On the Incarnation 54: “He became man that we might become God”), Augustine (Confessions 1.1: “our heart is restless”), Chrysostom (Homily on Matthew). Students summarize, note the main idea, and decide what is still relevant.
teach: The Fathers were early witnesses to Tradition (CCC 11, 78, 688, 2651). Their agreement is a mark of the Church’s faith (Dei Verbum 8).

Some Fathers are Doctors of the Church. Jerome translated the Vulgate; Augustine wrote the Confessions and City of God; Athanasius defended Nicaea; John Chrysostom (“golden mouth”) preached eloquently.
They wrote Scripture commentaries, creeds and catechetical lectures. Their approach is practical, pastoral and prayerful.
Men and women: also mention women like Monica, Macrina and Perpetua, who shaped them.
quiz: The Fathers were…|Popes only|Monks only|Early Church writers|Kings|2|CCC 11.
Augustine wrote…|Imitation of Christ|Spiritual Exercises|Summa|Confessions|3|Tradition.
Jerome translated…|The Koran|The Bible into Latin|The Talmud|The Iliad|1|Tradition.
lessons.life: Read a page from a Father in the Reading room.
lessons.saint: John Chrysostom: the golden-mouthed preacher who told the emperor’s court the truth.
misc: “The Fathers all agreed on everything.”
“They are only for scholars.”
lessons.mem: “O God, you have made us for yourself, and our heart is restless until it rests in you.” (St Augustine)
lessons.hook: Ask: “Who teaches the person who teaches you?” Read 2 Timothy 2:2 and talk about the chain from Paul to Timothy to others.
lessons.assess: Ask students to name three Fathers, one work or idea each, and why they matter.

script.open: Ask, “If you could read the letters of someone who knew Jesus’ friends, would you? The Church Fathers are those writers.”
teach: Say: “The Fathers of the Church are early Christian writers and bishops, from about AD 100 to 700, whose teaching is trusted as faithful. The Church honors them because they were close to the apostles’ time, they defended and explained the faith, and they were holy. They include the Apostolic Fathers, who knew the apostles’ disciples: Clement of Rome, Ignatius of Antioch, Polycarp. The Apologists, who defended the faith: Justin Martyr. And the great Fathers: in the East, Athanasius, Basil, Gregory of Nazianzus, Gregory of Nyssa and John Chrysostom; in the West, Ambrose, Jerome, Augustine and Gregory the Great.”

Say: “Each gave a gift. Athanasius defended the divinity of Christ. Basil wrote about the Holy Spirit and started monasteries. Chrysostom preached on Scripture. Ambrose taught the Mass and hymns. Jerome translated the Bible. Augustine, in his Confessions and City of God, explored grace, sin, and God’s love: ‘You have made us for yourself, and our hearts are restless until they rest in you.’ Gregory the Great organized the Church’s care for the poor and sent missionaries to England. The Church calls the greatest teachers Doctors of the Church.”

Say: “Why do the Fathers matter? When they agree, it is strong evidence of what the apostles taught. They show that the Catholic faith was not invented later. For example, on the Eucharist, Ignatius wrote that it is the flesh of Christ, and Justin that it is not common bread. On the Pope’s role, Irenaeus pointed to Rome. On Mary, Irenaeus called her the new Eve. They are also good reading: Augustine’s Confessions is still a best-seller. Their words fill the Liturgy of the Hours’ second reading.”
ask: Who are the Fathers of the Church? (Early Christian writers whose teaching is trusted.)
Name two Fathers and what they did. (Athanasius defended Christ’s divinity; Jerome translated the Bible.)
Why do they matter? (They show what the apostles taught.)
practice: Prepare cards with Father names and short quotes.
Teams match each Father to his contribution.
Pick one quote that speaks to you and copy it onto a bookmark.
Explain why you chose it.
script.close: Pray the prayer of Augustine: “You have made us for yourself, O Lord, and our hearts are restless until they rest in you.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Read a line from a Church Father in the Office of Readings.”

tryit: Match each Father to his work.
Quote one line.
Say why the Fathers matter.
lessons.saintStory:
John was born in Antioch around 349. His father died when he was young, and his mother Anthusa raised him. He studied rhetoric and could have had a career in law, but became a monk and hermit, living in a cave for two years until his health failed. He was ordained a priest, and for twelve years preached in Antioch, going through the Bible verse by verse. Because of his eloquence, he was called Chrysostom, “golden mouth.”
In 397 he was made archbishop of Constantinople, against his will. He reformed the clergy, sold the palace’s luxury items and gave the money to hospitals. He denounced the pride and cruelty of the rich, and criticized the empress Eudoxia. She had him exiled. He was brought back after an earthquake, then exiled again.
On a forced march in 407, in bad weather, he collapsed. His last words were: “Glory to God for all things.”

units.title: The Church in the Middle Ages
units.eq: What did the medieval Church achieve?

lessons.title: Monks and missionaries
lessons.idea: When persecution ended, some men and women withdrew to follow Christ more radically in prayer and work. Anthony in the Egyptian desert, Pachomius and Basil began communities; Benedict wrote a Rule built on “ora et labora” (pray and work). Monks preserved learning and carried the Gospel to new lands.
lessons.question: What did monasteries do?
lessons.activity: “A Benedictine day” (35 min). Examine the daily horarium of a monastery: Vigils, Lauds, work, lectio, Vespers, Compline. Students create a schedule that balances prayer, work and rest, and try silent lectio for five minutes.
teach: Consecrated life is a gift to the Church, a call to follow the evangelical counsels of poverty, chastity and obedience (CCC 914–933). Monastic life began with Anthony of Egypt (c. 270).
Benedict’s Rule (c. 530) stresses stability, obedience, hospitality and a balanced day: “Let nothing be preferred to the work of God.” Benedictines copied manuscripts and preserved classical texts.
Missionaries such as Patrick (Ireland), Augustine of Canterbury (England), Boniface (Germany) and Cyril and Methodius (Slavs) spread the Gospel.
Monastic communities still welcome guests. Invite students to consider visiting one.
quiz: Benedict wrote a…|Hymn|Rule|Creed|Gospel|1|Tradition.
Ora et labora means…|Read and write|Pray and work|Sing and dance|Eat and sleep|1|Rule.
Monasteries preserved…|Armies|Ships|Books and learning|Taxes|2|History.
lessons.life: Try a short daily rhythm of prayer and work.
lessons.saint: Benedict: the father of Western monks, who taught “pray and work.”
misc: “Monks run away from the world.”
“The Middle Ages were all darkness.”
lessons.mem: “If you would be perfect, go, sell what you possess and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me.” (Matthew 19:21)
lessons.hook: Ask: “What would you do with a day of silence? What would you pray for?” Read Matthew 19:21 about the rich young man.
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain “ora et labora” and how monks preserved the faith.

script.open: Ring a small bell at the start. Say, “A monk hears this bell eight times a day and stops what he is doing. What do you stop for?” Take answers and write them down.
teach: Say: “After Rome fell, Europe entered what we call the Middle Ages, about 500 to 1500. Monasteries became centers of faith and civilization. Monks copied manuscripts by hand, preserving the Bible and works of ancient writers. They farmed and drained marshes. They ran schools, hospitals and guesthouses. St. Benedict’s Rule gave them a balanced life: the day is divided into prayer (the Liturgy of the Hours), work and study (lectio divina). The monks took vows of stability, fidelity to monastic life, and obedience.”

Say: “Missionary monks spread the faith. Patrick, who as a young man was kidnapped and enslaved in Ireland, escaped, and later returned as bishop to convert the Irish. Irish monks such as Columba and Columbanus founded monasteries in Scotland and on the Continent. Pope Gregory the Great sent Augustine of Canterbury to England in 597. Boniface, an English monk, went to Germany and cut down the sacred oak at Geismar; he was martyred in 754. Cyril and Methodius evangelized the Slavs. These missionaries brought the Gospel to Europe and shaped the culture.”

Say: “In the 800s, Pope Leo III crowned Charlemagne as emperor on Christmas Day 800. Charlemagne supported schools and the Church. Later, new religious orders arose to renew the Church: the Cistercians, led by Bernard of Clairvaux, the Franciscans and Dominicans in the 1200s. The Middle Ages were not ‘dark’ to those who lived in them: they built cathedrals, founded universities and developed Gregorian chant. But they were not perfect: there was also corruption and war. The Church kept calling for reform.”
ask: What did Benedict’s Rule teach? (Pray and work, in community under an abbot.)
What did monasteries preserve? (Books, learning, farming, hospitality.)
Who evangelized Ireland? (Patrick.)
practice: Draw a clock of a monastery day: rising for Vigils, Lauds, work, Terce, Sext, None, work or study, Vespers, supper, Compline, sleep.
Mark prayer in one color, work in another, study in a third.
Write which part you would find hardest and which easiest.
Compare with your own day.
script.close: Pray Compline’s opening: “O God, come to my assistance. Lord, make haste to help me.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Pray and work: give your homework to God.”

tryit: Plan a day in a Benedictine monastery.
Mark prayer, work, study and rest.
Say what Benedict’s Rule gives.
lessons.saintStory:
Benedict was born around 480 in Nursia, Italy. As a student in Rome, he was shocked by the wild life of the other students and left to live as a hermit in a cave at Subiaco, where he stayed for three years. Others heard of his holiness and asked him to lead their monastery. Some monks, not liking his strictness, tried to poison him; the cup shattered when he made the sign of the cross over it.
He left and founded twelve small monasteries, then moved to Monte Cassino, where he wrote the Rule of Saint Benedict. It is a short, practical guide: the monks pray the Divine Office, work with their hands, read Scripture, eat together, and obey an abbot. It begins, “Listen carefully, my son, to the master’s instructions, and attend to them with the ear of your heart.”
Benedict died around 547. His Rule became the pattern for monasteries across Europe. His motto: Ora et labora, “pray and work.” He is patron of Europe.

lessons.title: Cathedrals, universities and saints
lessons.idea: The Middle Ages produced great cathedrals, universities and saints. Faith shaped art, music and learning. Thomas Aquinas, Francis of Assisi, Dominic and Catherine of Siena show different ways to holiness.
lessons.question: How did faith shape culture?
lessons.activity: “Cathedral tour” (30 min). Take a virtual tour of a Gothic cathedral. Students identify the cross-shaped plan, rose window, flying buttress, stained glass stories. Then read Psalm 27:4 and write a reflection: “What do I desire from the house of the Lord?”
teach: Faith inspired beauty: the Church’s tradition holds that beauty leads to God (CCC 2500–2503). Cathedrals were “Bibles in stone and glass” for a largely illiterate people.
Universities (Paris, Bologna, Oxford) grew out of cathedral schools. Aquinas’ Summa Theologiae joined faith and reason (CCC 31–35, 159).
Francis of Assisi embraced poverty and creation; Dominic founded the Order of Preachers; Catherine of Siena counseled popes. Women such as Hildegard and Clare shaped the age.
Be honest about the flaws (wars, corruption). The era was complex, not purely golden.

Aquinas wrote…|Imitation|Summa Theologiae|Confessions|Rule|1|History.
Gothic cathedrals aim at…|Heaven|Trade|Politics|Defense|0|History.
lessons.life: Look at a cathedral and name three symbols.
lessons.saint: Thomas Aquinas: a Dominican friar who joined faith and reason in the Summa.
misc: “Medieval people did not think; they only prayed.”
“Cathedrals were built to show off wealth.”
lessons.mem: “One thing have I asked of the Lord, that will I seek after: that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life.” (Psalm 27:4)
lessons.hook: Show a photo of Chartres or Notre-Dame’s interior. Ask: “What do you notice? Why do the windows soar up?”
lessons.assess: Ask students to name three medieval achievements and what they show about faith and culture.

script.open: Show a photo of Chartres Cathedral’s rose window. Say, “Someone spent a lifetime building this and never saw it finished. Why do people work on things that long?” Take answers.
teach: Say: “The high Middle Ages, about 1100 to 1300, were a time of great growth. Cathedrals rose, such as Chartres, Notre Dame and Cologne, with stained glass that taught the Bible to people who could not read. Pilgrims walked to Rome, Compostela and Jerusalem. Guilds of workers formed. And universities were founded: Bologna, Paris, Oxford and Cambridge. They were started by the Church, to study theology, law, medicine and the arts. The students were often clerics, and the professors included saints.”

Say: “New religious orders brought renewal. Francis of Assisi, who gave up wealth in 1206, started the Franciscans, who lived in poverty and preached in the streets. Dominic Guzmán founded the Dominicans to preach and teach. Clare of Assisi started the Poor Clares. These friars lived among the people in cities, not in remote monasteries. The Church also had saints like Elizabeth of Hungary, Louis IX of France, and Catherine of Siena.”

Say: “Thomas Aquinas taught that faith and reason do not conflict, since God is the author of both. Reason can show that God exists, and faith goes further, revealing truths like the Trinity. ‘Grace does not destroy nature but perfects it.’ In the Summa, he asks questions like ‘Does God exist?’ and follows a pattern: the question, the objections, the answer from authority (‘On the contrary…’), his own reply, and answers to each objection. He gave five ways to show that God exists, from motion, causation, contingency, degrees of perfection and design. The Church calls Thomas ‘Doctor of the Church’ and the Angelic Doctor.”
ask: What did the Church found in the Middle Ages? (Universities, hospitals, schools.)
What did Aquinas teach about faith and reason? (They cannot conflict, since God is the author of both.)
What were the new orders? (Franciscans and Dominicans.)
practice: Choose a question, like “Is it right to be angry?” or “Do we need God for morality?”.
Write the question at the top, then an objection, then “On the contrary…” and your reply.
Answer the objection.
Share with a partner, who argues the objection.
script.close: Pray the Tantum Ergo or Pange Lingua verse. Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Explain to someone why faith and reason go together.”

tryit: Read an article of the Summa in four steps.
Write your own objection and reply.
Say how faith and reason cooperate.
lessons.saintStory:
Thomas was born around 1225 in a castle in Italy, the son of a count. When he was about nineteen, he decided to join the Dominicans, a new order of preachers. His family was furious, since a noble son was supposed to become a Benedictine abbot. His brothers captured him and held him for over a year in the family castle, even sending a woman to tempt him. He drove her away with a burning stick. Eventually he escaped, and went to study with Albert the Great.
In class, his silence earned him the nickname “the dumb ox.” Albert said, “This ox will one day bellow so loud that it will fill the whole world.” Thomas taught in Paris and Italy, and wrote the Summa Theologiae, a vast, orderly summary of the faith. He used reason and the philosopher Aristotle to explain the faith.
In December 1273, after Mass, he stopped writing. “All that I have written seems like straw compared to what I have seen.” He died in 1274 on his way to a council. He wrote the hymns Pange Lingua and Tantum Ergo.

lessons.title: The East–West schism
lessons.idea: In 1054 the Churches of East and West formally divided, after centuries of growing apart. The causes included authority (the role of the Pope), the Filioque, language, culture and politics. Jesus’ prayer “that they may all be one” makes this a wound we pray to heal.
lessons.question: What caused the division?
lessons.activity: “Map the division” (30 min). Mark Rome and Constantinople, the Latin- and Greek-speaking worlds, the 1054 excommunications (Cardinal Humbert and Patriarch Michael Cerularius). List causes. Then read the 1965 lifting of excommunications (Paul VI and Athenagoras).
teach: The Eastern Orthodox and Catholic Churches share apostolic succession, sacraments and the Creed, but differ on papal primacy and jurisdiction, the Filioque and other points (CCC 817–819, 838).
The sack of Constantinople by Crusaders in 1204 deepened the rift. Attempts at reunion at Lyon (1274) and Florence (1439) did not last.
Today the Church seeks unity: Pope John Paul II said the Church must “breathe with both lungs.” Dialogue continues (CCC 820–822).
The 23 Eastern Catholic Churches are in full communion with Rome while keeping their own traditions.
talk: What do East and West share?

The Filioque concerns…|Icons|The Pope|Fasting|The procession of the Spirit|3|CCC 246.
Eastern Catholics are…|Protestant|Pagan|In communion with Rome|Orthodox|2|CCC 838.
lessons.life: Learn one Eastern Catholic Church’s name and customs.
lessons.saint: Cyril and Methodius: two brothers who gave the Slavs an alphabet and the liturgy in their own language.
misc: “The East left the Church over one word.”
“Orthodox are not Christian.”
lessons.mem: “That they may all be one, even as you, Father, are in me, and I in you.” (John 17:21)
lessons.hook: Read John 17:20–23 and ask what Jesus prays for. Then show a map of the Roman Empire divided and ask how distance might cause misunderstanding.
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain the main causes of the schism and one step toward healing.

script.open: Show a map of Europe and the Mediterranean. Ask, “Where was Rome? Where was Constantinople? Why might two such different cities, with different languages, have trouble staying together?”
teach: Say: “From the beginning, the Church had five great centers called patriarchates: Rome, Constantinople, Alexandria, Antioch and Jerusalem. In the East they spoke Greek, in the West Latin. Over centuries, they drifted apart in language, culture and politics. After Rome fell in the West, the Empire continued in the East, with its capital at Constantinople. There were disputes about the authority of the Pope, and about the words ‘and the Son’ (the filioque) added to the Creed in the West, stating that the Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son.”

Say: “In 1054, the Pope’s legate, Cardinal Humbert, and the patriarch of Constantinople, Michael Cerularius, excommunicated each other. This is called the East-West Schism. It was not a single event, but the end of a long period of division. In 1204, during the Fourth Crusade, Western crusaders sacked Constantinople, which deepened the wound. Attempts at reunion, such as the Council of Florence in 1439, did not hold. Today the Orthodox Churches (Greek, Russian, Serbian, Romanian and others) are separated from Rome.”

Say: “The Orthodox and Catholic Churches share much: the Creed, seven sacraments, bishops with apostolic succession, devotion to Mary and the saints, and the Real Presence. The main differences are the authority of the Pope and the filioque. Eastern Catholic Churches, such as the Maronite, Melkite and Ukrainian Greek Catholic, are in communion with Rome while keeping their own rites and traditions. Pope John Paul II said that the Church must ‘breathe with her two lungs,’ East and West. Popes and patriarchs have met in recent decades, and Catholics pray for unity.”
ask: When was the East-West Schism? (1054, ending a long drift.)
What do Orthodox and Catholics share? (Creed, sacraments, bishops, Mary and the saints.)
What are Eastern Catholic Churches? (Churches in communion with Rome with their own rites.)
practice: Draw a Venn diagram: Catholic, Orthodox, and what they share.
Fill in the overlap with at least six things we share, and the sides with differences.
Add one thing you admire about Eastern worship, such as icons, incense, or chanting.
Write a prayer for unity.
script.close: Pray: “That they may all be one.” (John 17:21.) Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Pray for Orthodox Christians.”

tryit: Map the East and the West.
List what the two churches share.
List what divided them.
lessons.saintStory:
Cyril and Methodius were brothers born in Thessalonica, a Greek city, in the ninth century. Cyril, whose baptismal name was Constantine, was a scholar. Methodius was an administrator. In 863 the prince of Moravia, in Central Europe, asked the Byzantine emperor for missionaries who could teach in the Slavic language.
The brothers created an alphabet for the Slavs, called Glagolitic, and translated the Gospels and liturgy into Old Church Slavonic. Some Latin-speaking clergy opposed them, arguing that liturgy should only be in Hebrew, Greek or Latin. The brothers traveled to Rome, and Pope Adrian II approved their work. Cyril died in Rome in 869. Methodius was made archbishop and continued to work for sixteen more years.
They are patrons of Europe, with Benedict, and honored by both Catholics and Orthodox. Their story belongs to the time when East and West were still together.

units.title: Reformation and renewal
units.eq: How did the Church respond to division?

lessons.title: The Reformation
lessons.idea: The Reformation began in 1517 when Martin Luther challenged the sale of indulgences. It grew into a wider break from Rome about authority, Scripture, justification and the sacraments, giving rise to Lutheran, Reformed and Anglican traditions. It left lasting wounds in Christian unity.
lessons.question: What issues divided?
lessons.activity: “Key issues chart” (30 min). Students build a chart with columns: issue, Reformers’ position, Catholic position (authority: sola scriptura vs. Scripture and Tradition; justification: faith alone vs. faith working through love; sacraments: two vs. seven; the Mass; the papacy). Include real abuses: indulgence sellers, simony, clerical corruption.
teach: The abuses were real. Many Catholics, including saints, asked for reform. Luther’s Ninety-five Theses (1517) challenged indulgence preaching (CCC 1471–1479). The break widened with the Diet of Worms (1521).

Reformers stressed Scripture alone, faith alone, grace alone. Catholics affirm Scripture, Tradition and the Magisterium, and justification by grace through faith that works in love (CCC 80–82, 1987–1995).
Henry VIII’s break with Rome (1534) was political. Calvin’s Geneva developed Reformed theology. Wars of religion followed.
Since Vatican II the Church recognizes our separated brothers and sisters as Christians and seeks unity (CCC 817–819).

Luther posted…|10 Commandments|95 Theses|12 Articles|7 Sacraments|1|History.
Catholics and Protestants share…|The Mass|Papacy|Baptism and Scripture|Purgatory|2|CCC 818.
lessons.life: Pray for Christian unity.
lessons.saint: Peter Canisius: a Jesuit who taught the faith by catechism and kindness in a divided Germany.
misc: “Luther simply wanted to leave the Church.”
“All Reformers agreed.”
lessons.mem: “I appeal to you, brethren… that there be no dissensions among you, but that you be united in the same mind.” (1 Corinthians 1:10)
lessons.hook: Ask: “When is it right to speak out about a problem in an institution you love? What can go wrong?” Introduce Luther as a case.
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain three issues in the Reformation and how Catholics responded.

script.open: Ask, “What do you do when you love something that has serious problems, like a school or team you belong to? Leave, or work for change? Why?” Take answers.
teach: Say: “By the early 1500s, the Church needed reform. Some bishops were worldly and some clergy were poorly trained. Church offices were bought and sold (simony). Many people were not well instructed in the faith. In 1517, Pope Leo X was raising money to rebuild St. Peter’s Basilica, and preachers like Johann Tetzel were selling indulgences in a way that suggested forgiveness could be purchased. An Augustinian friar and professor named Martin Luther posted 95 theses at Wittenberg, questioning this practice. He wanted a debate.”

Say: “It escalated. Luther also taught that we are justified by faith alone (sola fide), that Scripture alone is the authority (sola scriptura), and rejected the Pope’s authority and most sacraments. He was excommunicated in 1521. In Switzerland, Zwingli and John Calvin led other movements. In England, Henry VIII broke with Rome in 1534 to secure a divorce, making himself head of the Church; Thomas More and John Fisher died rather than accept it. The movement spread, and Europe was torn by wars of religion. Today there are about 900 million Protestants.”

Say: “The Church’s view is that the Reformers’ complaints about abuses were often right, but their remedy broke the unity of the Church and departed from some teachings. Catholics teach that we are justified by grace through faith, but faith must be alive in love and good works (James 2:24). Scripture and Tradition together, interpreted by the Magisterium, are the rule of faith. Today Catholics and Protestants have much in common: faith in Christ, the Trinity, Scripture and Baptism. In 1999, Catholics and Lutherans issued a Joint Declaration on Justification. We are called to respect and to pray for unity, and to avoid caricatures.”
ask: What sparked the Reformation in 1517? (The sale of indulgences and Luther’s 95 theses.)
What are two Reformation slogans? (Sola fide, sola scriptura.)
What do Catholics and Protestants share? (Faith in Christ, the Trinity, Scripture, Baptism.)
practice: Make a table with three columns: causes, responses, results.
Fill in with at least four items each.
Mark in green what is genuine reform and in red what departed from Catholic teaching.
Write a sentence on how to talk respectfully with a Protestant friend.
script.close: Pray: “Lord, heal the wounds of division.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Ask a Christian from another tradition what they love about their church.”

tryit: List the causes of the Reformation.
Mark what was real reform and what departed from the faith.
Write what Catholics and Protestants share.
lessons.saintStory:
Peter Canisius was born in 1521 in the Netherlands, the year Martin Luther was condemned at the Diet of Worms. He studied law, and then joined the Jesuits, the first Dutchman to do so. He was sent to Germany, where many were leaving the Catholic Church, and spent his life there.
He was a professor, preacher and adviser. He wrote three catechisms, clear and simple, that were used for centuries; by one count he had more than 200 editions. He founded schools. He believed the best way to respond was with charity and clear teaching, not insults. He insisted that Catholics should be fair toward Protestants, and he asked that sermons not be used to attack.
He worked at the Council of Trent and helped keep Southern Germany Catholic. He died in 1597 and is a Doctor of the Church.

lessons.title: The Council of Trent
lessons.idea: The Council of Trent (1545–1563) responded to the Reformation by clarifying doctrine and reforming the Church. It defined the canon, the sacraments, justification and the Mass, and set up seminaries, a catechism and stricter discipline.
lessons.question: What did Trent do?
lessons.activity: “Trent summary” (30 min). Students read a summary of Trent’s decrees and sort them into doctrine and reform. Then compare the Roman Catechism (1566) to today’s Catechism of the Catholic Church. Read 2 Timothy 4:1–5.
teach: Trent affirmed seven sacraments, transubstantiation, the Mass as sacrifice and the canon of 73 books (CCC 120, 1376, 1129).
It taught justification by grace, with cooperation of the free will (CCC 2008–2010). It rejected the claim that grace is only external.
Reforms: seminaries for priests, bishops to reside in their dioceses, the Roman Catechism, a standard missal. These produced saints like Charles Borromeo.
The Counter-Reformation also brought Baroque art and new orders (Jesuits, Capuchins) and renewed missions.

lessons.life: Read part of the Roman Catechism.
lessons.saint: Ignatius of Loyola: a wounded soldier who became a master of discernment and founded the Jesuits.
misc: “Trent invented new doctrines.”
“Trent was only a reaction against Protestants.”
lessons.mem: “Preach the word; be ready in season and out of season.” (2 Timothy 4:2)
lessons.hook: Ask: “If your school needed to fix problems and explain its rules, what would you do?” Compare to Trent’s doctrine and reform.
lessons.assess: Ask students to name two doctrinal and two disciplinary results of Trent.

script.open: Read aloud the opening line of the decree on the Eucharist from Trent, or a short paragraph from the Roman Catechism. Say, “Hear the tone. These are bishops trying to put a house in order.” Ask what they were afraid of losing.
teach: Say: “The Church answered the Reformation with the Council of Trent, held in Trent, Italy, in three periods from 1545 to 1563 under Popes Paul III, Julius III and Pius IV. It is sometimes called the Counter-Reformation or Catholic Reformation. The Council did two things: it clarified Catholic doctrine, and it reformed abuses.”

Say: “Doctrine: Scripture and Tradition are both sources of revelation; the Church interprets. Justification comes by grace, and good works are fruit and merit. There are seven sacraments. The Mass is a true sacrifice, and Christ is truly present in the Eucharist (transubstantiation). The Church confirmed the canon of 73 books, and affirmed the Latin Vulgate. Reform: bishops must live in their dioceses and preach. Seminaries must be set up in every diocese to train priests; before this, many priests had no formal training. Selling church offices and indulgences was condemned. The Council issued the Roman Catechism, a standard Missal (1570), and the Breviary.”

Say: “New and renewed orders drove the reform. The Jesuits, founded by Ignatius of Loyola, were educators and missionaries. The Capuchins renewed the Franciscans. Teresa of Avila and John of the Cross reformed the Carmelites. Philip Neri founded the Oratory. Charles Borromeo, Francis de Sales and Vincent de Paul led by example. The Church also saw the great art of the Baroque era, which proclaimed the faith in beauty. The reform was a renewal from within, which lasted over three centuries until Vatican II.”
ask: What did Trent do? (Clarified doctrine and reformed abuses.)
What were seminaries for? (Training priests.)
Who founded the Jesuits? (Ignatius of Loyola.)
practice: Prepare a chart: Problem, Trent’s response.
Fill in: uneducated priests / seminaries; confusion about doctrine / Roman Catechism; absent bishops / residence; abuses of indulgences / reform.
Try Ignatius’s Examen for five minutes: thank God for the day, review your day, notice what was life-giving and what was not, ask forgiveness, resolve for tomorrow.
Share one insight.
script.close: Pray the Suscipe of Ignatius: “Take, Lord, receive all my liberty.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Do the Examen each night.”

tryit: List the reforms of Trent.
Match each to a problem.
Try the Examen.
lessons.saintStory:
Ignatius was born in 1491 in the Basque region of Spain, a young nobleman and soldier, proud and vain. In 1521, at the battle of Pamplona, a cannonball shattered his leg. During a long recovery at the castle of Loyola, he asked for books of romance, but the only ones available were a life of Christ and lives of the saints. He noticed that when he thought of worldly deeds, he was excited and then empty; when he thought of following Christ like the saints, he felt lasting peace. This was the start of his method of discernment.
He gave up his sword, spent time at Manresa in prayer, wrote the Spiritual Exercises, and studied in Paris. There he gathered a small group of friends, including Francis Xavier, and in 1540 the Pope approved their order, the Society of Jesus. The Jesuits took a special vow of obedience to the Pope and ran schools around the world.
Ignatius died in 1556. His motto: Ad majorem Dei gloriam, “for the greater glory of God.”

lessons.title: Missionaries and saints
lessons.idea: New religious orders and missionaries carried the Gospel across the world. Ignatius of Loyola founded the Jesuits; Francis Xavier traveled to India and Japan; Teresa of Ávila and John of the Cross renewed the Carmelites; Francis de Sales taught holiness for everyone.
lessons.question: Who were Ignatius and Teresa?
lessons.activity: “Biography presentations” (35 min). Each student presents a 2-minute biography: Ignatius, Francis Xavier, Teresa of Ávila, John of the Cross, Francis de Sales, Rose of Lima, Isaac Jogues. Include a quote and a lesson for today. Link to Matthew 28:19.
teach: The Church is missionary by nature (CCC 849–856). The age of exploration brought both heroic missionaries and entanglement with colonialism; some defended native peoples (Bartolomé de las Casas).
Ignatius’ Spiritual Exercises teach discernment. Teresa and John teach contemplative prayer (CCC 2709–2719). Francis de Sales taught the “devout life” for ordinary people (CCC 2013).
Missionary martyrs include the North American Martyrs, Japanese martyrs and many in China and Africa. The Church grows by witness.
Name some saints from your own culture to show how the Gospel takes root in each people.
quiz: Ignatius founded the…|Benedictines|Jesuits|Dominicans|Franciscans|1|History.
Teresa of Avila reformed the…|Jesuits|Franciscans|Carmelites|Augustinians|2|History.
Francis Xavier went to…|Iceland|India and Japan|Egypt|Brazil only|1|History.
lessons.life: Research a missionary saint.
lessons.saint: Francis Xavier: a Jesuit who carried the Gospel to India and Japan.
misc: “Missionaries were only agents of empire.”
“Only priests can be missionaries.”
lessons.mem: “Go therefore and make disciples of all nations.” (Matthew 28:19)
lessons.hook: Show a world map with lines to Asia, Africa and the Americas. Ask: “What would it take to go there in 1550?”
lessons.assess: Ask students to present a saint’s contribution and what it teaches today.

script.open: Show a world map. Ask, “In 1492, Columbus sailed. How did the faith get to the Americas, Asia and Africa? Who went?” Take guesses.
teach: Say: “The age of exploration, from 1492, opened new worlds. Spain and Portugal sent explorers, and the Church sent missionaries. Franciscans, Dominicans, Augustinians and Jesuits traveled to Mexico, Peru, Brazil, India, China, Japan, the Philippines and Africa. In 1531, Mary appeared at Guadalupe to Juan Diego, a native man, and millions of Native Americans converted. Missionaries learned local languages and wrote dictionaries and grammars. They established schools and hospitals.”

Say: “There were also failures. Some colonizers abused and enslaved native peoples, and some missionaries went along with this. But others defended the natives. Bartolomé de las Casas, a Dominican, denounced the cruelty. Pope Paul III in 1537 declared that the Indians are truly men and must not be enslaved. Peter Claver served enslaved Africans. Jesuits in Paraguay built ‘reductions,’ self-governing communities that protected native peoples. Matteo Ricci in China adapted, wearing Chinese scholars’ robes and learning the language and philosophy. Not all of this mission history is glorious. The Church acknowledges the sins of her members.”

Say: “Missionary saints include Francis Xavier, Rose of Lima (the first saint of the Americas), Martin de Porres, Junípero Serra, Isaac Jogues and the Canadian martyrs, Kateri Tekakwitha, the Japanese martyrs of Nagasaki (1597, 26 martyrs; and later hidden Christians for 250 years), Paul Miki, and the Korean and Vietnamese martyrs. The missions made the Church truly worldwide. Jesus told his disciples to go to all nations. Every Catholic shares in this mission by prayer, giving and witness.”
ask: Who defended the rights of native peoples? (Las Casas, Pope Paul III, Peter Claver.)
Who was the first saint of the Americas? (Rose of Lima.)
What did Matteo Ricci do in China? (Adapted to Chinese culture.)
practice: Give each pair a blank world map.
Mark: Goa and Japan (Xavier), Mexico (Guadalupe), Peru (Rose of Lima), China (Ricci), Paraguay (reductions), Canada (martyrs).
Beside each, write the missionary and one fact.
Write a sentence on what you admire about missionaries and what troubles you.
script.close: Pray the Memorare for missionaries or “Lord, send workers into your harvest.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Pray for missionaries and give to the missions.”

tryit: Map the missions.
Mark each missionary and place.
Say what they brought and how they adapted.
lessons.saintStory:
Francis Xavier was born in 1506 in Navarre, Spain. He was a bright, ambitious student at the University of Paris, hoping for fame. His roommate Ignatius of Loyola kept asking him, “What does it profit a man if he gains the whole world and loses his soul?” In time, Francis was won over. In 1534 he and Ignatius and five others took vows at Montmartre.
In 1541 he sailed for India, a thirteen-month voyage. He worked in Goa, then among the poor fishermen on the southern coast, where he taught the Our Father and Creed by song and had children go door to door ringing a bell. He then went on to Malacca, the Moluccas, and in 1549 to Japan, where he learned that the local culture respected scholars and rank. He planned to enter China but died in 1552 on an island off its coast, at forty-six.
He is patron of missions, and is said to have baptized tens of thousands.

units.title: The modern Church
units.eq: How does the Church meet the modern world?

lessons.title: Vatican II
lessons.idea: The Second Vatican Council (1962–1965), called by John XXIII, renewed the Church’s life and mission. It issued sixteen documents, including four constitutions: on the Church (Lumen Gentium), Divine Revelation (Dei Verbum), the Liturgy (Sacrosanctum Concilium) and the Church in the modern world (Gaudium et Spes).
lessons.question: What changed?
lessons.activity: “Four constitutions” (35 min). Groups take one constitution, read a short excerpt and list its main ideas and a practical result (Mass in the vernacular, a call to holiness for all, Scripture’s place, dialogue with the world). Create a one-page summary and present.
teach: The Council did not change doctrine but deepened and renewed its expression (CCC 10–11). Lumen Gentium: the Church as mystery and People of God, the universal call to holiness (CCC 770–776, 2013).

Dei Verbum: Scripture and Tradition; Sacrosanctum Concilium: full, conscious, active participation in the liturgy (CCC 1071–1075). Gaudium et Spes: the Church’s joy and hope, grief and anguish for all people.
Other documents: on ecumenism (Unitatis Redintegratio), non-Christian religions (Nostra Aetate), religious freedom (Dignitatis Humanae).
Be honest that interpretations differ, and encourage reading the texts themselves.
quiz: Vatican II began under…|Pius XII|John XXIII|Paul VI|Leo XIII|1|History.
Sacrosanctum Concilium concerns…|The world|The Church|The liturgy|Scripture|2|History.
Gaudium et Spes concerns…|Scripture|Liturgy|Priests|The Church in the modern world|3|History.
lessons.life: Read a short passage from Gaudium et Spes.
lessons.saint: John XXIII: the “good pope” who opened the windows of the Church.
misc: “Vatican II abolished the old Mass or doctrine.”
“The Council changed Church teaching on everything.”
lessons.mem: “I came that they may have life and have it abundantly.” (John 10:10)
lessons.hook: Say: “Open the windows,” which is what John XXIII said about the Council. Ask what that image suggests.
lessons.assess: Ask students to name the four constitutions and one lasting fruit of each.

script.open: Open a window in the classroom, or show a picture of one. Ask, “What happens when a room is stuffy and we open a window? John XXIII used this picture for the Church.”
teach: Say: “The Second Vatican Council met in Rome from 1962 to 1965 under John XXIII and then Paul VI. About 2,500 bishops from around the world attended. Pope John said its aim was aggiornamento, ‘bringing up to date,’ and not changing the faith, but presenting it in a way the modern world can hear. The council produced 16 documents. It did not change doctrine, but renewed the Church’s life.”

Say: “The four major documents are called constitutions. Lumen Gentium, on the Church, describes her as the People of God, with a universal call to holiness, and the role of the laity. Dei Verbum, on Revelation, explains Scripture and Tradition, and encourages all to read the Bible. Sacrosanctum Concilium, on the liturgy, led to the Mass in local languages, greater participation, and a richer use of Scripture. Gaudium et Spes, on the Church in the modern world, says ‘the joys and hopes, the griefs and anxieties of the people of this age… are the joys and hopes, the griefs and anxieties of the followers of Christ.’”

Say: “Other documents deal with ecumenism (Unitatis Redintegratio), non-Christian religions (Nostra Aetate, which condemned antisemitism and affirmed what is true in other religions), religious freedom (Dignitatis Humanae), and the role of laity (Apostolicam Actuositatem). Many Catholics today can still be confused about what Vatican II taught. Pope Benedict XVI said we should read it with a ‘hermeneutic of reform’ in continuity with the whole tradition. The council was not a break with the past but a renewal. Its main points: holiness for all, active participation in the liturgy, reading Scripture, dialogue with the world, and mission.”
ask: Who called Vatican II? (John XXIII.)
What are the four constitutions? (Lumen Gentium, Dei Verbum, Sacrosanctum Concilium, Gaudium et Spes.)
What does Gaudium et Spes say? (The joys and hopes of people are those of Christians too.)
practice: Make a four-row chart: document, subject, one change.
Fill from the lesson and the Catechism.
Look for one visible sign of Vatican II in your parish: Mass in English, lay readers, the Bible readings.
Write one thing the Council asks of you.
script.close: Pray: “Come, Holy Spirit, renew your Church.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Ask an older person what changed after Vatican II.”

tryit: List the four constitutions of Vatican II.
Match each to a change.
Find one at your parish.
lessons.saintStory:
Angelo Roncalli was born in 1881 to a poor farming family in northern Italy. He became a priest, served as a stretcher-bearer in World War I, then as a Vatican diplomat in Bulgaria, Turkey and Greece. During World War II he helped save Jewish refugees. He became cardinal of Venice, and in 1958, at seventy-six, was elected pope, expected to be a short “caretaker.”
Three months later, he announced a council. Many were surprised; no council had been held since 1870. He said he wanted to “open the windows of the Church to let in some fresh air.” Vatican II opened in October 1962. He was warm, jovial and humble, and was loved by people of all faiths.
John XXIII died of cancer in 1963, after the first session. He was named a saint in 2014, together with John Paul II. His last words in a letter: “Be good, be gentle, be at peace.”

lessons.title: Social teaching
lessons.idea: Catholic social teaching applies the Gospel to society. Its seven themes — dignity of the person, family and community, rights and responsibilities, option for the poor, dignity of work, solidarity, care for creation — guide how we treat people and build the common good.
lessons.question: What are the themes?
lessons.activity: “Match themes to examples” (30 min). Cards with themes and cases (a living wage, a refugee family, a polluted river, a bullied classmate, a school food drive). Students match, explain and propose a step they can take.
teach: The tradition begins with Leo XIII’s Rerum Novarum (1891) on the rights of workers and continues through Pius XI, John XXIII, Paul VI, John Paul II, Benedict XVI and Francis (CCC 2419–2425).
Principles: the dignity of every person (CCC 1700–1709), the common good (CCC 1905–1912), subsidiarity (CCC 1883–1885), solidarity (CCC 1939–1942), preferential love for the poor (CCC 2443–2449).
The Church teaches that work is for the person, and that creation is a gift to be shared and protected (CCC 2426–2436, 2415–2418).
Social teaching is not partisan. It challenges every ideology.
quiz: Rerum Novarum was written by…|Paul VI|Francis|Leo XIII|Pius XII|2|History.
The common good is…|Conditions that let all flourish|Law only|Wealth|The majority wish|0|CCC 1906.
Solidarity means…|Competition|Charity only|Isolation|Sharing burdens|3|CCC 1939.
lessons.life: Do one act of solidarity.
lessons.saint: Katharine Drexel: an heiress who gave away a fortune to educate Native and Black Americans.
misc: “Social teaching is just politics.”
“Charity is enough; justice is not the Church’s business.”
lessons.mem: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me to proclaim good news to the poor.” (Luke 4:18)
lessons.hook: Read Luke 4:18–19. Ask: “What does ‘good news to the poor’ mean in practice?”
lessons.assess: Ask students to name four principles and apply two to a case.

script.open: Display a news photo of a food bank line and one of a corporate headquarters. Say, “Both are true about our economy. Who should speak for the people in the first picture?” Take answers.
teach: Say: “In 1891, Pope Leo XIII wrote Rerum Novarum, ‘On the New Things,’ the first great social encyclical. The Industrial Revolution had brought wealth for some and misery for many workers in factories. Leo said that workers have rights: to a just wage, safe conditions and to form unions. Property is a right, but it has a social purpose. Both socialism and unchecked capitalism are wrong. Popes since then have updated the teaching: Pius XI, John XXIII, Paul VI, John Paul II (Centesimus Annus), Benedict XVI, and Francis (Laudato Si’).”

Say: “The Church has seven themes of Catholic social teaching. One: the life and dignity of the human person. Two: call to family, community and participation. Three: rights and responsibilities. Four: the option for the poor and vulnerable, putting the needs of the poor first. Five: the dignity of work and the rights of workers. Six: solidarity, we are one human family. Seven: care for God’s creation. These come from Scripture and reason. They are tools for judging social problems.”

Say: “The principles also include the common good, the conditions that let everyone flourish, and subsidiarity, which means decisions should be made at the lowest level able to handle them, so that families and communities are not replaced by the state. Pope Francis in Laudato Si’ calls us to hear ‘both the cry of the earth and the cry of the poor.’ Social teaching is not a political party, but it does challenge every party. It asks us to see Christ in the poor, to work for justice, and to live simply.”
ask: What was Rerum Novarum about? (The rights of workers.)
What is the option for the poor? (Giving priority to the needs of the poor.)
What is subsidiarity? (Decisions should be made at the lowest competent level.)
practice: Write the seven themes on cards, and the examples on others: food bank, minimum wage, recycling, pro-life work, refugee welcome, volunteer in the community, voting.
Teams match them.
Choose a real issue in your community and apply two principles to it.
Plan one action.
script.close: Pray: “Lord, make us instruments of your justice and peace.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Support a cause that helps the poor.”

tryit: Match each principle of social teaching to an example.
Apply two to a real issue.
Plan one action.
lessons.saintStory:
Katharine Drexel was born in 1858 in Philadelphia, to one of America’s richest banking families. Her parents were generous Catholics who opened their home to the poor twice a week. As a young woman, Katharine toured Europe, and then visited the Western reservations where she saw the poverty of Native Americans. She asked Pope Leo XIII to send missionaries; he replied, “Why not become a missionary yourself?”
At thirty-three, she took vows, and founded the Sisters of the Blessed Sacrament for Indians and Colored People. She used her inheritance to build schools and missions across the country, including Xavier University in New Orleans, the first Black Catholic university in the United States. She faced opposition and threats, including from groups who tried to burn down a school.
She gave away about twenty million dollars in her lifetime. She died in 1955, at ninety-six, and was named a saint in 2000.

lessons.title: The Church worldwide
lessons.idea: The Catholic Church includes 24 self-governing Churches in full communion with the Pope: the Latin Church and 23 Eastern Catholic Churches. They share one faith and sacraments but have their own liturgies, laws and traditions. Revelation 7:9 pictures every nation worshiping together.
lessons.question: How many Churches are in communion?
lessons.activity: “Churches on a map” (30 min). Students mark the Latin Church and several Eastern Catholic Churches (Maronite, Melkite, Ukrainian Greek Catholic, Syro-Malabar, Chaldean, Coptic, Armenian) on a world map. Add one distinctive feature each (liturgical language, icons, married clergy, chrismation of infants).
teach: The Church is catholic in her unity and diversity (CCC 830–838). The Eastern Catholic Churches use the Byzantine, Alexandrian, Antiochene, Armenian and Chaldean rites (CCC 1200–1206).
Many Eastern Catholic Churches ordain married men to the priesthood; infants receive Baptism, Chrismation and Communion together (CCC 1290, 1233).
Eastern Orthodox Churches are not in full communion but share much. Learning from them enriches our faith.
Visit an Eastern Catholic parish if possible.
talk: Why do we have many rites?
quiz: The Church has…|One rite|Many rites in one faith|Two rites|No rites|1|CCC 1203.
Eastern Catholics are led by…|Rome only|Their own bishops united with Rome|Nobody|Kings|1|CCC 882.
The Divine Liturgy is the Eastern name for…|The Mass|Marriage|Baptism|Confession|0|Tradition.
lessons.life: Visit an Eastern Catholic church or watch a Divine Liturgy.
lessons.saint: Josaphat Kuntsevych: an Eastern-rite archbishop who died working for unity.
misc: “Catholic means Roman Catholic only.”
“Eastern Catholics are Orthodox who converted.”
lessons.mem: “After this I looked, and behold, a great multitude that no one could number, from every nation, from all tribes and peoples and languages.” (Revelation 7:9)
lessons.hook: Display the Sign of the Cross in different languages or rites. Ask: “Is it the same prayer?” Explore unity in diversity.
lessons.assess: Ask students to name five Churches, their rite and one distinctive practice.
