script.open: Ask, “How many Catholics are in the world? Where do they live? Guess.” Take guesses. “About 1.4 billion. Where do most live?”
teach: Say: “Today the Catholic Church has about 1.4 billion members, about one in six people. More than 60 percent are in the Americas and Africa. Latin America has the most Catholics, with Brazil and Mexico leading. Africa is growing fastest. In Asia, the Philippines is largely Catholic, and there are minorities in India, Vietnam, Korea and China. In Europe, the numbers have fallen. The center of the Church’s population has moved from Europe to the Global South.”

Say: “The Church is one, but with many rites. The Latin (Roman) Rite is the largest. The Eastern Catholic Churches are 23 Churches in communion with the Pope, with their own liturgy, law and traditions: Ukrainian, Maronite, Melkite, Syro-Malabar, Syro-Malankara, Chaldean, Coptic, Ethiopian and others. They have their own patriarchs and bishops, and some have married priests. We should respect and learn about these Churches, since they bring the Church’s ancient traditions.”

Say: “In many places, the Church is under pressure. In China, the Church is divided between government-registered and underground communities. In the Middle East, Christians have fled war and persecution; in Nigeria, Pakistan and elsewhere, Christians face violence. In Europe and North America, many have left the practice of the faith. The Church is also growing in places like Africa and parts of Asia. The Pope serves as the visible sign of unity. Through Catholic Relief Services, missionary societies and the Propagation of the Faith, we support the Church worldwide. We’re one family.”
ask: Where are most Catholics today? (The Americas and Africa.)
What are Eastern Catholic Churches? (Churches in communion with Rome with their own rites.)
How can we support the worldwide Church? (Pray, give, learn, and serve.)
practice: Divide a world map into continents.
For each, write an approximate Catholic number, a country, and a saint or event.
Choose one place where Christians suffer, and write a prayer for them.
Look up one Eastern Catholic Church and write three facts.
script.close: Pray for the Church throughout the world and for persecuted Christians. Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Learn about an Eastern Catholic Church.”

tryit: Match each continent to its Catholics.
Name a saint from each.
Say what the Church’s worldwide shape means.
lessons.saintStory:
Josaphat Kuntsevych was born around 1580 in what is now Ukraine, then part of Poland-Lithuania. As a young man he was a merchant’s apprentice, and then became a Basilian monk in the Eastern tradition. In 1596, some years before, the Union of Brest had united many Orthodox bishops in the region with Rome, creating the Ukrainian Greek Catholic Church, which kept its Eastern liturgy. But the union was controversial; many Orthodox opposed it.
Josaphat became archbishop of Polotsk and worked to bring unity. He preached, reformed the clergy, and wrote a catechism. His work made him popular with many, but angered opponents. In 1623, a mob in Vitebsk attacked his residence and killed him with an axe.
He was the first Eastern Catholic to be formally canonized by Rome, in 1867. His story reminds us of the beauty and the pain of the divisions among Christians.

lessons.title: The Holy Spirit in the Church
lessons.idea: The Holy Spirit is the soul of the Church. He sanctifies her, teaches her all truth, gives her gifts and charisms, and unites her to Christ. Jesus promised the Spirit as Advocate and Spirit of truth.
lessons.question: How do we see the Spirit?
lessons.activity: “Study Pentecost and beyond” (30 min). Read Acts 2 and John 14–16. Students chart the Spirit’s work: teaches, recalls Jesus’ words, convicts of sin, guides to truth, empowers witnesses. Add examples from Church history (councils, saints) and personal life.
teach: The Spirit is “the soul of the Church” (CCC 797–798). He builds up the Body through the sacraments, the Word, charisms and ministries (CCC 799–801).
Jesus promised, “He will teach you all things and bring to your remembrance all that I have said to you” (John 14:26). The Spirit guides the Church’s Magisterium (CCC 91–93).
Charisms are special graces for the good of the Church (1 Corinthians 12; CCC 799–801). They must be discerned and ordered by pastors.
Teach epiclesis: the Church calls on the Spirit at every sacrament (CCC 1105–1109).
talk: What is the soul of the Church?
How do you see the Spirit?
quiz: The soul of the Church is…|The Holy Spirit|The Pope|The building|The saints|0|CCC 797.
The Spirit gives…|Land|Money|Power|Gifts and charisms|3|CCC 799.
The Spirit teaches…|Violence|Silence|Fear|All truth|3|John 16:13.
lessons.life: Pray Veni Creator.
lessons.saint: Basil the Great: the bishop who wrote the classic book on the Holy Spirit.
misc: “The Spirit works only in emotional experiences.”
“Only a few are given the Spirit.”
lessons.mem: “The Advocate, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, he will teach you all things.” (John 14:26)
lessons.hook: Read John 14:16–17. Ask: “What does ‘Advocate’ mean?” (someone called alongside to help). The Spirit never leaves the Church.
lessons.assess: Ask students to describe three ways the Spirit acts in the Church.

script.open: Wave a sheet of paper or blow gently across a candle flame. Say, “The Spirit is described as wind and as fire. What can you see of wind or fire? What do you see only by what it does?” Take answers.
teach: Say: “The Holy Spirit is the third Person of the Trinity: God, equal to the Father and the Son. The Creed says, ‘I believe in the Holy Spirit, the Lord, the giver of life, who proceeds from the Father and the Son, who with the Father and the Son is adored and glorified, who has spoken through the prophets.’ He is not an impersonal force. He is a Person, with whom we can have a relationship. Jesus called him the Advocate, Paraclete (John 14:16), the Spirit of truth.”

Say: “Scripture uses symbols of the Spirit. Water: he gives life and cleanses (John 7:37-39). Anointing with oil: he strengthens and consecrates. Fire: he purifies and sets hearts aflame (Acts 2). Cloud and light: his presence and power, as at Jesus’ Transfiguration. The seal: he marks us permanently in Baptism, Confirmation and Orders. The hand: laying on of hands. The dove: peace and new creation, at Jesus’ baptism. Wind or breath: he gives life, as when God breathed on Adam and Jesus breathed on the apostles (John 20:22).”

Say: “What does the Spirit do? He inspired the Scriptures, speaking through the prophets. He overshadowed Mary. He descended on Jesus at his baptism. At Pentecost, he came upon the Church and still guides her: he leads the Church into all truth (John 16:13), he gives life in the sacraments, he forms the saints, he gives gifts and charisms to the faithful for service. He dwells in us as in a temple (1 Corinthians 6:19). He prays in us when we do not know how (Romans 8:26). The Church is the work of the Spirit. We invoke him often: ‘Come, Holy Spirit.’”
ask: Who is the Holy Spirit? (The third Person of the Trinity, God.)
Name three symbols of the Spirit. (Water, fire, dove, oil, wind.)
What does the Spirit do in the Church? (Guides, gives life in the sacraments, forms saints.)
practice: Make a chart: Symbol, Scripture, What it shows.
Fill in water, oil, fire, dove, wind, seal, hand.
Draw each one.
Write a prayer to the Holy Spirit using one of the symbols.
script.close: Pray the sequence “Come, Holy Spirit” or the Veni Creator. Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Pray to the Holy Spirit before homework.”

tryit: Fill in the Holy Spirit’s names and symbols.
Link each to a Scripture passage.
Say what the Spirit does in the Church.
lessons.saintStory:
Basil was born around 330 in Caesarea, Cappadocia (now Turkey), to a family of saints: his grandmother Macrina, his parents, and his brothers Gregory of Nyssa and Peter of Sebaste, and sister Macrina were all honored as saints. He studied in Athens, where he met Gregory of Nazianzus. Giving up a career in rhetoric, he traveled to visit monks in Egypt and Syria, and then started a community on his family’s estate.
In 370 he became bishop of Caesarea. He fought against Arianism, which denied the divinity of Christ, and against emperors who favored it. He set up a huge complex called the Basiliad that included a hospital, a hostel for travelers and a workshop for the poor. When a famine struck, he preached and organized relief.
His book On the Holy Spirit defended the Spirit’s full divinity: the Spirit is to be worshiped and glorified with the Father and the Son. He died in 379. His liturgy is still used in Eastern churches.

lessons.title: The gifts and fruits
lessons.idea: Isaiah names seven gifts of the Spirit (wisdom, understanding, counsel, fortitude, knowledge, piety, fear of the Lord). Paul lists the fruits (love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, generosity, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control and others). The gifts are given, the fruits ripen.
lessons.question: What are they?
lessons.activity: “Memorize and apply” (30 min). Students memorize the seven gifts and the fruits. Then play a matching game: scenarios (a hard decision, bullying, a test) with the gift that helps. Pray the Veni Creator or Come Holy Spirit.
teach: The seven gifts (Isaiah 11:1–3) make us docile to the Spirit’s promptings (CCC 1830–1831). Wisdom and understanding perfect faith, counsel and fortitude guide action, knowledge helps us see things as God does, piety deepens love and reverence, fear of the Lord is wonder and awe.
The fruits of the Spirit are “the first fruits of eternal glory” (CCC 1832): charity, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, generosity, gentleness, faithfulness, modesty, self-control, chastity.
Gifts are received at Baptism and strengthened in Confirmation. Fruits show the Spirit at work.
Distinguish gifts from charisms and from virtues.
talk: How do gifts differ from fruits?
quiz: There are…|Three gifts|Twelve gifts|Seven gifts|Nine gifts|2|CCC 1831.
Fortitude is…|Counsel|Courage|Knowledge|Wisdom|1|CCC 1831.
A fruit of the Spirit is…|Joy|Anger|Pride|Fear|0|Galatians 5:22.
lessons.life: Pray daily for one gift.
lessons.saint: Joan of Arc: a farm girl who showed fortitude, counsel and piety at nineteen.
misc: “Fear of the Lord means being terrified.”
“Gifts are for the holy; fruits are optional.”
lessons.mem: “The fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control.” (Galatians 5:22–23)
lessons.hook: Show a fruit tree. Ask: “How do you know what kind of tree it is?” By its fruit. Read Galatians 5:22–23.
lessons.assess: Ask students to recite the seven gifts and give an example of a fruit in daily life.

script.open: Hand out cards with the seven gifts written on them and ask each student to pick the one they think they need most this month. Keep them for the practice. Take a quick show of hands for each gift.
teach: Read Isaiah 11:1-3. Say: “‘The Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him, the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and might, the spirit of knowledge and the fear of the Lord.’ This is the source of the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit. They are permanent dispositions that make us ready to follow the Spirit’s promptings. We receive them in Baptism, and they are strengthened in Confirmation. Jesus had them in fullness.”

Say: “The seven gifts: Wisdom lets us see all things in relation to God and his plan. Understanding helps us grasp the truths of faith. Counsel helps us choose rightly in hard decisions. Fortitude (courage) gives strength to do good despite fear. Knowledge helps us see created things as they relate to God. Piety (reverence) is love and devotion toward God as Father. Fear of the Lord is awe and wonder before God, and a sorrow at offending him. It is not terror but reverence. The gifts perfect the virtues and make us docile to the Spirit.”

Read Galatians 5:22-23. Say: “The fruits of the Spirit are the results when the Spirit works in us: ‘love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control.’ The Church’s traditional list has twelve: charity, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, generosity, gentleness, faithfulness, modesty, self-control, chastity. The gifts are like the root system, the fruits are what we can see. You can tell a tree by its fruit. Ask: What fruit do others see in me?”
ask: Name the seven gifts. (Wisdom, understanding, counsel, fortitude, knowledge, piety, fear of the Lord.)
What is fear of the Lord? (Awe and reverence, not terror.)
What is the difference between gifts and fruits? (Gifts are dispositions; fruits are the results we show.)
practice: Make a card for each gift.
On each, write a short definition, a moment from Joan’s life or another saint’s, and a way you might need it this week.
Underline the one you most need.
Pray for it with a partner.
script.close: Pray: “Come, Holy Spirit, give me your seven gifts.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Pray each day for one gift.”

tryit: Match each gift to a moment in Joan’s life.
Write one example for yourself.
Name the fruit that follows.
lessons.saintStory:
Joan was born around 1412 in Domrémy, in northeastern France, to a peasant family, during the Hundred Years’ War, when England controlled much of France. She was a devout girl who heard voices, which she said were St. Michael, St. Catherine and St. Margaret, telling her to help the Dauphin Charles to be crowned king.
At sixteen, she went to the local commander, who scoffed at her. But she persisted, and was taken to Charles, and examined by theologians. She was given armor and a banner, and at seventeen led troops to lift the siege of Orléans in nine days. She then accompanied Charles to Reims, where he was crowned in 1429.
In 1430, she was captured by Burgundians and sold to the English. At a trial for heresy at Rouen, she answered clearly and bravely, despite being an unlettered girl. She was burned at the stake on May 30, 1431, aged about nineteen, calling out “Jesus.” In 1456 a retrial declared her innocent; she was canonized in 1920.

lessons.title: The sacrament of Confirmation
lessons.idea: Confirmation completes baptismal grace. The bishop anoints the forehead with chrism and says, “Be sealed with the Gift of the Holy Spirit.” We are strengthened, bound more closely to the Church, and sent to bear witness.
lessons.question: What happens?
lessons.activity: “Prepare the rite” (35 min). Walk through the rite: presentation of candidates, homily, renewal of baptismal promises, laying on of hands, anointing with chrism, general intercessions. Students write what they will say in their own words, and prepare a service project.
teach: Confirmation, with Baptism and the Eucharist, completes initiation (CCC 1285). It imprints an indelible spiritual mark and increases the gifts of the Spirit (CCC 1302–1305).
The essential rite is anointing with chrism, together with the words (CCC 1300). In the Latin Church, the bishop is the ordinary minister (CCC 1312–1314).
Effects: deeper rootedness in divine sonship, closer union with Christ, increase of the Spirit’s gifts, a more perfect bond with the Church, strength to witness (CCC 1303).
Requirements: to be baptized, in a state of grace, with proper instruction. A sponsor accompanies the candidate (CCC 1307–1311).
quiz: Confirmation is a sacrament of…|Marriage|Initiation|Healing|Service|1|CCC 1212.
The anointing is with…|Chrism|Salt|Water|Incense|0|CCC 1297.
A sponsor…|Judges|Pays|Helps the candidate|Replaces the priest|2|CCC 1311.
lessons.life: Write a letter to the bishop asking for Confirmation.
lessons.saint: Cyril of Jerusalem: a bishop who explained Confirmation to the newly baptized.
misc: “Confirmation is when I choose to be Catholic.”
“I can skip Confirmation and still be fully initiated.”
lessons.mem: Be sealed with the Gift of the Holy Spirit. (Rite of Confirmation)
lessons.hook: Ask: “What do you need to be ready for a big responsibility?” (training, support, strength). Confirmation is God’s strengthening.
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain the rite, its effects and what it asks of them.

script.open: Ask, “Why do athletes and soldiers get a uniform or special oil or mark before they begin? What does it signal?” Take answers.
teach: Read Acts 8:14-17 and 19:1-6. Say: “In Samaria, those baptized by Philip did not yet receive the Spirit until Peter and John arrived and laid hands on them. In Ephesus, Paul laid hands on baptized disciples, and the Holy Spirit came on them. From apostolic times, the Church has joined Baptism with a laying on of hands and prayer for the Spirit. This is the sacrament of Confirmation. Together with Baptism and the Eucharist, it is one of the sacraments of Christian initiation.”

Say: “In the Latin Church, the bishop is the ordinary minister of Confirmation, though priests can confirm with permission (for example, at the Easter Vigil for adults). In the Eastern Churches, the priest confirms (called chrismation) right after Baptism, even for infants. The essential rite has two parts: the laying on of hands (an extended gesture over all the candidates) and the anointing of the forehead with sacred chrism, with the words ‘Be sealed with the Gift of the Holy Spirit.’ The chrism is blessed by the bishop at the Chrism Mass during Holy Week.”

Say: “What does it do? It increases and deepens the grace of Baptism. It gives a special strength of the Holy Spirit to spread and defend the faith by word and deed. It seals the person with an indelible mark, so it is only received once. A candidate needs to be baptized, in the state of grace, prepared and instructed, and choose a sponsor, who should be a practicing Catholic, to accompany them. Many choose a Confirmation name, a saint to be a patron. Confirmation is not graduation from the Church. It is the beginning of mission.”
ask: Who usually confirms? (The bishop.)
What are the two parts of the rite? (Laying on of hands and anointing with chrism.)
What do the words say? (Be sealed with the Gift of the Holy Spirit.)
practice: Number cards: Presentation of candidates, Homily, Renewal of baptismal promises, Laying on of hands, Anointing with chrism, Sign of peace, Prayer of the faithful.
Put them in order.
Beside each, write what it means.
Write a preparation plan: which saint you’ll choose, who your sponsor is, a service project, and a promise to pray.
script.close: Pray: “Send forth your Spirit, and they shall be created, and you shall renew the face of the earth.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Talk with your sponsor or a parent about your Confirmation.”

tryit: Walk through the rite of Confirmation.
Match each sign to its meaning.
Write your own preparation plan.
lessons.saintStory:
Cyril was born around 313 and was bishop of Jerusalem from about 350. He was exiled from his see three times during the Arian controversies. In Jerusalem, he oversaw the preparation of adults for Baptism at Easter. In Lent he gave lectures, called the catechetical lectures, to the candidates on the Creed. During the week after Easter, he gave the newly baptized a series of talks, called mystagogical catecheses, explaining the sacraments they had received.
He described the anointing after Baptism: “As Christ after his baptism and the coming of the Holy Spirit went out and conquered the adversary, so you also, after holy Baptism and the sacramental chrism, put on the whole armor of the Holy Spirit.” He explained that the oil is no mere ointment, but the gift of Christ and the Holy Spirit, and that the forehead, ears, nostrils and breast are anointed.
He died in 386 and is a Doctor of the Church. His talks give a window into how the early Church celebrated these sacraments.

units.title: Living a moral life
units.eq: How do we live as disciples?

lessons.title: Conscience and freedom
lessons.idea: Freedom is not doing whatever we want but the power to choose the good. Conscience is the inner judgment that helps us see what is right, and it must be formed. True freedom grows as we practice virtue.
lessons.question: What is freedom?
lessons.activity: “Case study debate” (35 min). Present cases (peer pressure to cheat, a rumor, a risky dare, honesty about a mistake). Students apply the steps of conscience: pray, learn what the Church teaches, seek advice, weigh consequences, choose. Discuss which choices lead to freedom.
teach: Freedom is “the power, rooted in reason and will, to act or not to act, to do this or that” (CCC 1731). It grows to perfection when directed to God (CCC 1731, 1744). “For freedom Christ has set us free” (Galatians 5:1).
The human act is judged by its object, intention and circumstances (CCC 1750–1756). A good intention does not make a bad act good.
Conscience must be formed; one is obliged to follow a certain conscience (CCC 1776–1785). Ignorance may lessen responsibility, but we should seek the truth.
Freedom is limited by habits, fear and social pressure, but never destroyed (CCC 1735–1748).
quiz: Freedom is…|Having money|Power to choose the good|Avoiding rules|Doing anything|1|CCC 1731.
Conscience must be…|Silent|Hidden|Formed|Ignored|2|CCC 1783.
A person must always follow…|A friend|The crowd|Feeling|A certain judgment of conscience|3|CCC 1790.
lessons.life: Examine a decision with the Church’s teaching.
lessons.saint: Blessed Franz Jägerstätter: an Austrian farmer who followed his conscience against Hitler.
misc: “Freedom is doing what I want.”
“If I feel good about it, my conscience is clear.”
lessons.mem: “For freedom Christ has set us free; stand firm therefore.” (Galatians 5:1)
lessons.hook: Present two images: a train on tracks and a train off the tracks. “Which is free to go where it was made to go?” Freedom is for something.
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain true freedom and the steps of forming a conscience with an example.

script.open: Read this case aloud: a friend says, ‘My conscience is clear, so it is fine.’ Ask, “Is a clear conscience always a right conscience?” Let two students argue each side for one minute.
teach: Read Romans 2:14-16. Say: “Paul writes that the law is ‘written on their hearts, while their conscience also bears witness.’ Conscience is the judgment of reason by which we recognize the moral quality of an act, past or about to be done. The Catechism says it is ‘a judgment of reason whereby the human person recognizes the moral quality of a concrete act.’ Vatican II called conscience ‘the most secret core and sanctuary of a man, where he is alone with God.’ We must always follow our conscience, and we must always form it.”

Say: “Conscience can be mistaken. It must be formed by Scripture, the teaching of the Church, prayer, advice from wise people and examination. A poorly formed conscience can be culpable if the ignorance is our fault. Jägerstätter’s conscience was well formed: he read the Bible and the teaching of the Church, prayed, and asked for advice. How do we form conscience? Study the Gospel and the Ten Commandments. Learn the Church’s teaching (the Catechism). Pray for light. Ask for advice. Examine the day. Avoid occasions of sin. And be honest with yourself.”

Say: “Freedom is not doing whatever we want, but the power to choose the good. The more we do good, the freer we become; sin enslaves. Jesus said, ‘The truth will make you free.’ (John 8:32) We must always do what we judge to be right, and never do something we think is wrong. A conscience can be certain, doubtful or erroneous. If doubtful, we must seek to clarify. We are responsible for our acts. Three sources of a moral act: the object (what we do), the intention (why we do it), and the circumstances. An act is good only if all three are good. A good end does not justify a bad means.”
ask: What is conscience? (A judgment of reason about the goodness of an act.)
How do we form conscience? (Scripture, Church teaching, prayer, advice, examination.)
What are the three sources of morality? (Object, intention, circumstances.)
practice: Give a dilemma: a friend asks you to copy your homework; a group wants to post a mean joke about a classmate; you find a wallet with cash.
Work through the steps: What is the act? What is my intention? What are the circumstances? What does the Church teach? Who could I ask?
Decide what to do.
Write one habit of conscience-formation you will start.
script.close: Pray: “Lord, give me a well-formed conscience and the courage to follow it.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Do a short examination of conscience each night.”

tryit: Work through the steps of forming conscience.
Apply them to a real dilemma.
Write one habit to keep.
lessons.saintStory:
Franz Jägerstätter was born in 1907 in a small village in Austria, the son of an unmarried farm maid, and raised by his grandmother. As a young man, he had a wild streak, but after marrying Franziska in 1936 and going on a honeymoon pilgrimage to Rome, he grew deeply devout. He became the village sexton, and prayed daily.
When Germany annexed Austria in 1938, he was the only person in his village to vote against it. In 1943, he was called up for military service. He believed that the war was unjust, and that he could not take the oath to Hitler. His pastor and bishop urged him to think of his family. His wife supported him. “I cannot and may not take an oath in favor of a government that is fighting an unjust war.”
He was arrested, tried and sentenced to death. He was beheaded on August 9, 1943, at thirty-six. He was beatified in 2007, and his story has become a model of conscience.

lessons.title: Virtue and sin
lessons.idea: Virtue builds the good; sin harms. Virtues are habits that make doing good easier. The capital sins — pride, avarice, envy, wrath, lust, gluttony and sloth — are root vices. The remedy is grace and daily practice.
lessons.question: How do we grow?
lessons.activity: “Growth plan” (30 min). Each student identifies one virtue to grow and the opposing vice, plans three daily practices, a support (friend, prayer, sacrament) and a way to track progress. Read Romans 7:15–25 as a sign that struggle is normal.
teach: Virtue is a firm disposition to do good (CCC 1803). Human virtues are acquired; theological virtues are gifts (CCC 1804–1829).
Sin is an offense against God, reason and truth (CCC 1849). It creates a tendency to more sin (vice). The capital sins give rise to others (CCC 1866).
Romans 7: “I do not do what I want, but I do the very thing I hate.” Paul shows both struggle and hope: “Thanks be to God through Jesus Christ.”
Address both pride and scrupulosity. God’s grace strengthens; examine yourself without despair.
quiz: Capital sins are…|Imaginary|Venial sins only|Greatest crimes|Sources of other sins|3|CCC 1866.
A virtue is…|A feeling|A good habit|A thought|A rule|1|CCC 1803.
Pride is…|Disordered love of self|Courage|Joy|Humility|0|CCC 1866.
lessons.life: Choose a virtue to oppose a vice.
lessons.saint: John Vianney: a parish priest who became a saint through patience, fasting and hours in the confessional.
misc: “I can overcome all sin by willpower.”
“Everyone sins, so it doesn’t matter.”
lessons.mem: “Thanks be to God through Jesus Christ our Lord!” (Romans 7:25)
lessons.hook: Ask: “What does an athlete do to become strong?” Daily practice. The same is true for virtues; vice is a habit too.
lessons.assess: Ask students to name the seven capital sins with their opposing virtues.

script.open: Write ‘habit’ on the board and have students list three habits they have that help them and three that hurt them. Ask, “How did you build these? Can you undo them?” Collect a few.
teach: Say: “A virtue is a habit of doing good. It is a firm disposition we build by practice, with God’s help. There are human virtues, which we acquire by effort, and theological virtues, which God gives. The four cardinal virtues are the hinges on which the others turn: Prudence: knowing the right thing to do. Justice: giving each what is due. Fortitude: courage in difficulty. Temperance: moderation in pleasure. The three theological virtues are faith, hope and charity (love), which are infused by God and have God for their object. Paul wrote, ‘So faith, hope, love abide, these three; but the greatest of these is love.’”

Say: “The opposite of virtue is vice, a habit of doing wrong. Sin is a failure to love. We have already learned that sin may be mortal or venial. The Church also speaks of the seven capital sins, those which lead to other sins: pride, avarice (greed), envy, wrath (anger), lust, gluttony, sloth. Each has a corresponding virtue: pride and humility, greed and generosity, envy and kindness, anger and patience, lust and chastity, gluttony and temperance, sloth and diligence. Pride is the root of the others.”

Say: “How do we grow in virtue? By practice: every time we choose the good, it gets easier. By grace in the sacraments and prayer. By avoiding occasions of sin. By having a daily examination of conscience. By having good friends and role models. Ben Franklin made a chart for virtues; so can you. Also: sin is not only what we do, but what we fail to do (sins of omission). And we can share in the sins of others by encouraging them. We resist temptation as Jesus did, and we use the sacrament of Confession to be restored.”
ask: Name the four cardinal virtues. (Prudence, justice, fortitude, temperance.)
Name the three theological virtues. (Faith, hope, charity.)
How many capital sins are there? (Seven.)
practice: Prepare cards of actions: sharing lunch, gossip, finishing homework, angry outburst, honesty on a test, skipping Mass.
Sort each into a virtue or vice, naming which one.
Match the vices to the capital sins, and the corresponding virtue.
Choose a virtue to practice this week, and plan a daily tracking mark.
script.close: Pray the Act of Contrition. Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Track your virtue each day.”

tryit: Sort acts and habits into virtues and vices.
Name the capital sin behind each.
Choose one virtue to practice.
lessons.saintStory:
Jean-Marie Vianney was born in 1786 in France, in a farming family, during the French Revolution, when Mass was often illegal. He struggled in school, especially with Latin, and nearly failed to be ordained. When he was finally ordained at twenty-nine, he was sent to Ars, a tiny village of about 230 people that had grown cold in the faith.
He lived very simply, ate little, often just boiled potatoes, and slept little. He visited every family, taught the children and spent many hours in prayer. People started to attend Mass, and the dances and taverns emptied. Word spread, and eventually 20,000 pilgrims a year came to Ars to go to confession to him. He spent sixteen to eighteen hours a day in the confessional.
He died in 1859, and is patron of parish priests. He taught: “The sinner does not have to be pursued; God’s mercy is waiting.”

lessons.title: Respect for life and the person
lessons.idea: Every human life is sacred from conception to natural death because each person is made in God’s image. The fifth commandment forbids murder, abortion, euthanasia and suicide, and calls us to protect life and care for the vulnerable.
lessons.question: Why life?
lessons.activity: “Service project” (35 min). Plan a project that honors life: visit a nursing home, help a pro-life pregnancy center, make cards for the sick, write to a lonely person. Prepare respectfully and discuss how to speak with charity about hard topics.
teach: Human life is sacred (CCC 2258). Direct and intentional killing of an innocent person is gravely wrong (CCC 2268–2269). Abortion is a grave offense (CCC 2270–2275).

Euthanasia and assisted suicide are morally unacceptable; legitimate refusal of burdensome treatment is allowed (CCC 2276–2279). Suicide is contrary to love of self and God, though the Church prays for those who die this way (CCC 2280–2283).
The Church also protects life by defending the poor, the immigrant, the prisoner, and by promoting peace (CCC 2302–2317). The death penalty is now judged inadmissible (CCC 2267).
Offer compassion to women facing difficult pregnancies and to those who have suffered abortion or loss; Project Rachel offers healing.
talk: What does the Church teach about the dying?
quiz: Human life is sacred from…|Age 5|Conception to natural death|Age 18|Birth|1|CCC 2270.
The Church teaches that euthanasia is…|Optional|A right|Fine|Morally unacceptable|3|CCC 2277.
We should care for…|Nobody|The powerful|The famous|The poor and the weak|3|CCC 2448.
lessons.life: Support a pro-life ministry.
lessons.saint: Damien of Molokai: a priest who lived with those with leprosy and became one of them.
misc: “The Church cares about life only before birth.”
“All end-of-life care must be continued.”
lessons.mem: “For you formed my inward parts; you knit me together in my mother’s womb.” (Psalm 139:13)
lessons.hook: Read Psalm 139:13–16 aloud. Ask: “What does this say about how God sees each of us before anyone else does?”
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain the dignity of life and two ways to protect it.

script.open: Ask, “Who do people in our society treat as if they matter less? Who do they ignore?” Let students answer; list on the board. “These are the people the Church says have equal dignity.”
teach: Say: “The Church teaches that every human being has an inherent dignity because every person is made in God’s image and redeemed by Christ. This dignity does not depend on age, ability, race, wealth or usefulness. It comes from God, and no one can take it away. This is the foundation of Catholic moral teaching. We have seen how the fifth commandment protects life from conception to natural death. But dignity also means how we treat people: with respect, honesty and justice.”

Say: “Here are areas where dignity is at stake. At the beginning of life: abortion and embryo destruction. At the end: euthanasia and assisted suicide. The Church supports palliative care, which eases suffering, but not killing. In war: just war theory, and the protection of civilians. In society: racism, human trafficking, slavery, abuse of the poor and immigrants. The death penalty: the Catechism says it is ‘inadmissible’ because it is an attack on the inviolability and dignity of the person. Also bullying, hate speech and pornography, which treat persons as objects.”

Say: “The Church also teaches about the proper care for the body. We must care for our health, avoid addictions (drugs, alcohol abuse), and use medicine for healing. Organ donation can be an act of charity. Medical research is good when it respects life and dignity. Technology, including social media and AI, should serve human persons. The golden rule: ‘Whatever you wish that men would do to you, do so to them.’ (Matthew 7:12) And Jesus’ teaching of the Good Samaritan: our neighbor is anyone in need.”
ask: Where does human dignity come from? (Being made in God’s image and redeemed by Christ.)
What does palliative care do? (Eases suffering without killing.)
Who is my neighbor? (Anyone in need.)
practice: Brainstorm situations where dignity is at risk (bullying, ignoring a classmate, online humiliation, treatment of the elderly or disabled).
For each, write what respecting dignity looks like.
Choose one and plan a specific action for this week.
Share one.
script.close: Pray: “Lord, help me see your image in every person.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Greet someone who is often ignored.”

tryit: List the situations where human dignity is at stake.
Apply the principle of dignity.
Plan one act of respect.
lessons.saintStory:
Jozef De Veuster was born in Belgium in 1840, the son of a farmer, and became a priest of the Sacred Hearts, taking the name Damien. He was sent to Hawaii in 1864. In 1873, he volunteered to go to Molokai, an isolated peninsula where people with leprosy, then called Hansen’s disease, were sent, mostly to die. Conditions were terrible: little food, shelter or order.
Damien built houses, a church and a water system; he dressed wounds, dug graves and built coffins. He did not keep away. He shared meals with the sick, and wrote, “I make myself a leper with the lepers to gain all to Jesus Christ.” One day in 1885, while soaking his feet in very hot water, he felt nothing. He realized that he had caught the disease. In his next sermon, he began, “We lepers…”
Damien died in 1889, at forty-nine. Mahatma Gandhi later said that he was one of the heroes of humanity. He was named a saint in 2009.

units.title: Prayer and mission
units.eq: How do we live our faith?

lessons.title: Ways of praying
lessons.idea: Prayer takes three main expressions: vocal prayer with words, meditation with thought, and contemplation, a silent gaze of love. All three have a place in a mature life of prayer.
lessons.question: What is your method?
lessons.activity: “Try three forms” (35 min). Stations: vocal (pray the Our Father slowly), meditation (read Matthew 6:25–34 and imagine the scene), contemplation (sit with the Jesus Prayer: “Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me”). Students write a brief reflection after each.
teach: Vocal prayer unites body and spirit; Jesus taught us the Our Father (CCC 2700–2704). Meditation seeks to understand the why and how of the Christian life (CCC 2705–2708).
Contemplative prayer is “a gaze of faith fixed on Jesus… a silent love” (CCC 2709–2719). It is a gift, not a technique.
Obstacles: distraction, dryness, acedia (CCC 2729–2733). Remedies: persevering, humility, simple trust.
Encourage a daily rhythm: morning offering, mealtime, a quiet ten minutes, examen at night.
quiz: Vocal prayer uses…|Silence|Dance|Art|Words|3|CCC 2700.
Meditation is…|Daydreaming|Seeking understanding|Reading news|Napping|1|CCC 2705.
Contemplation is…|Singing|Silent love|Argument|Math|1|CCC 2709.
lessons.life: Try 3 minutes of silent prayer daily.
lessons.saint: Teresa of Avila: a Carmelite who taught that prayer is friendship with God.
misc: “If my mind wanders, I’m failing.”
“Meditation means emptying my mind.”
lessons.mem: “Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me, a sinner.” (The Jesus Prayer)
lessons.hook: Say the Jesus Prayer slowly for one minute in silence. Ask what they noticed. Introduce the three expressions.
lessons.assess: Ask students to describe each expression of prayer and which they will practice this week.

script.open: Say, “Close your eyes for one minute. Notice what your mind does when you try to be silent.” After a minute, ask what they noticed. Say, “This is prayer’s first challenge.”
teach: Say: “The Catechism says that prayer is ‘the raising of one’s mind and heart to God or the requesting of good things from God.’ (CCC 2559) It is a relationship, God’s thirst meeting ours. Prayer is a gift, a covenant and a communion. There are three expressions of prayer: vocal prayer, meditation and contemplation. Vocal prayer uses words, aloud or silently, like the Our Father or the Rosary. Meditation is thinking about God’s word, using the mind and imagination, as in lectio divina. Contemplation is simply being with God, gazing in love, often in silence. Teresa described it as ‘an act of love.’”

Say: “There are five forms of prayer. Blessing and adoration: we worship God for who he is. Petition: we ask for what we need. Intercession: we ask for others. Thanksgiving: we give thanks. Praise: we glorify God for his own sake. We can remember them with the acronym ACTS or PRAY: Praise, Repent, Ask, Yield. Prayer should include silence. The psalms and the Mass shape our prayers. And we also use sacramentals: a crucifix, an icon, a rosary, holy water.”

Say: “Prayer can be difficult: distractions, dryness, doubt, being busy, discouragement. Teresa had them for years. Her advice: persevere. Start small, with a fixed time and place. Use a book if you need to. Begin with the Sign of the Cross and a prayer to the Holy Spirit. When distracted, gently return. Don’t expect feelings. Pray even when it feels dry; fidelity matters more than feeling. Jesus said, ‘Ask, and it will be given you.’ (Luke 11:9) The Our Father is the model of Christian prayer.”
ask: What are the three expressions of prayer? (Vocal, meditation, contemplation.)
Name the five forms of prayer. (Blessing/adoration, petition, intercession, thanksgiving, praise.)
What should we do when prayer is dry? (Persevere; fidelity matters more than feelings.)
practice: Rotate through four stations, three minutes each: vocal prayer (the Our Father slowly), meditation (a Gospel verse), contemplation (silence before a cross), praise (a psalm or hymn).
At each, write one sentence about what happened.
Choose the one that helps you most.
Make a plan for ten minutes a day.
script.close: Pray the Bookmark of Teresa: “Let nothing disturb you, let nothing frighten you; all things pass; God alone is enough.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Pray ten minutes daily.”

tryit: Try each of the four forms of prayer.
Write what you noticed.
Choose one to practice daily.
lessons.saintStory:
Teresa was born in 1515 in Avila, Spain. At twenty, she entered the Carmelite convent of the Incarnation. For almost twenty years, she struggled to pray; she had a lively mind that wandered. The convent was relaxed, with many visitors. Then, standing before a statue of the wounded Christ, she was overcome, and began a deeper life of prayer.
She described her experiences and her advice in her books, The Way of Perfection and The Interior Castle. She compared the soul to a castle with many rooms, with God at the center. She said prayer is “nothing else than an intimate sharing between friends; it means taking time frequently to be alone with him who we know loves us.”
With John of the Cross, she reformed the Carmelites, founding seventeen convents, traveling over rough roads in a covered cart. She was funny and practical: “From silly devotions and sour-faced saints, good Lord, deliver us!” She died in 1582 and was the first woman declared a Doctor of the Church.

lessons.title: The Mass and Adoration
lessons.idea: The Eucharist feeds us as the bread of life, and Eucharistic adoration extends the Mass by prayer before the Blessed Sacrament. Jesus said, “Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life.”
lessons.question: Why adoration?
lessons.activity: “Visit the Blessed Sacrament” (30 min). Take students to church for a silent visit. Teach how to genuflect, kneel and pray: adoration, thanksgiving, sorrow, petition (ACTS). Afterwards, write a prayer and share what struck them.
teach: The Eucharist is the Body and Blood, Soul and Divinity of Christ (CCC 1374). In John 6 Jesus says his flesh is “true food” (John 6:55) and many disciples left rather than accept it.
Eucharistic worship outside Mass is a prolongation of Mass (CCC 1378–1381). The tabernacle, Benediction and Forty Hours devotion honor Christ present.
The fruits of Communion: union with Christ, forgiveness of venial sin, protection from mortal sin, unity of the Church (CCC 1391–1397).
Teach the Church’s norms of preparation and reverence (CCC 1385–1389).
quiz: Adoration is…|Magic|Habit|Worship of Christ in the Eucharist|Worship of bread|2|CCC 1378.
The Blessed Sacrament is kept in the…|Sacristy|Pew|Chalice|Tabernacle|3|CCC 1379.
Benediction ends with…|Homily|Gloria|A blessing|Creed|2|Tradition.
lessons.life: Spend 15 minutes in adoration.
lessons.saint: Clare of Assisi: a woman who drove away an army by holding up the Blessed Sacrament.
misc: “Adoration is staring at bread.”
“Communion is optional if I go to Mass.”
lessons.mem: “I am the living bread that came down from heaven; if anyone eats of this bread, he will live forever.” (John 6:51)
lessons.hook: Ask: “What does food do?” (feeds, strengthens, shares). Read John 6:35 and 6:51 and note what Jesus says about himself as food.
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain Real Presence and how adoration relates to Mass.

script.open: Show a picture of a monstrance, if available. Ask, “What is this? Have you ever seen it? What do we do in front of it?”
teach: Say: “The Mass is the center of Catholic life. We have called it the source and summit. Each part of the Mass has its own purpose. The Introductory Rites gather us. The Liturgy of the Word has God speak to us. The Liturgy of the Eucharist unites us to Christ’s sacrifice. The Communion Rite feeds us. The Concluding Rites send us. We should prepare before Mass: fast for one hour, be in the state of grace, arrive early, and pray. We take part actively by responding, singing, listening and offering ourselves with the bread and wine.”

Say: “The Mass is a sacrifice, a memorial and a banquet. It is the same sacrifice as Calvary. Christ is the priest and the victim. The priest acts in his person. The Mass is not a new sacrifice, but makes the one sacrifice present. We join our lives to it. We are also fed with his Body and Blood. The Eucharist unites us with Christ, with each other, and strengthens us. It forgives venial sins and preserves us from mortal sin.”

Say: “Outside of Mass, the Blessed Sacrament is reserved in the tabernacle, for Communion to the sick and for adoration. Eucharistic adoration is prayer before the Blessed Sacrament, exposed in a monstrance or in the tabernacle. We kneel, we watch and wait. Jesus asked the apostles at Gethsemane, ‘Could you not watch one hour with me?’ Benediction is a short service in which the priest blesses the people with the Blessed Sacrament. Many saints, like Clare, Thomas Aquinas, Padre Pio and Mother Teresa, drew their strength from adoration. The Eucharistic Procession on Corpus Christi shows our faith publicly.”
ask: Is the Mass a new sacrifice? (No, it makes present the one sacrifice of Calvary.)
What is Eucharistic adoration? (Praying before the Blessed Sacrament.)
What is Benediction? (A blessing with the Blessed Sacrament.)
practice: Visit the church if you can, or look at a picture of the Blessed Sacrament.
Be silent for five minutes. Use the prompts: Jesus, I believe you are here. Thank you for… Help me with… I love you.
Afterward write a prayer of adoration in a few sentences.
Plan a time this month to visit the Blessed Sacrament.
script.close: Pray the Tantum Ergo or: “Jesus, I adore you.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Visit Jesus in the tabernacle this week.”

tryit: Spend a quiet time before a monstrance image.
Write a prayer of adoration.
Plan a visit to the Blessed Sacrament.
lessons.saintStory:
Clare was born in 1193 in Assisi, to a noble family. At eighteen, she heard Francis of Assisi preach, and was inspired by his poverty. On Palm Sunday night in 1212, she slipped out of her home, met Francis at the Portiuncula chapel, and had her hair cut off. She went to a Benedictine convent, and finally to San Damiano, where she lived in poverty with the other women who joined her, the Poor Clares.
In about 1240, according to tradition, an army of Saracen mercenaries was attacking Assisi. They broke into the convent. Clare, sick, asked to be carried to the door, and holding the monstrance with the Blessed Sacrament, she prayed for her sisters. The soldiers fled.
She lived at San Damiano for forty years, much of it ill in bed. She died in 1253. She is often shown with a monstrance, and is patron of television, since on her deathbed she saw and heard Mass on the wall of her room, when she was too ill to go to church.

lessons.title: Called to evangelize
lessons.idea: Every baptized Catholic shares in the Church’s mission to evangelize. We witness by how we live and by what we say, with respect and joy. Evangelization begins with a personal encounter with Jesus.
lessons.question: How will you witness?
lessons.activity: “Witness project” (35 min). Students write a 30-second testimony (“how God has been present to me”), then plan a witness project: a service day, inviting a friend to Mass, a social media post, or a prayer group. Practice with partners.
teach: Evangelization means proclaiming the Gospel to bring people to Christ (CCC 849–856, 863). All the baptized share in this mission through their baptismal priesthood (CCC 900, 905).
The Church teaches that mission respects freedom (CCC 160, 2104–2109). Pope Francis stresses that the Church grows by attraction, not proclaiming at others.

Witness of life, loving service and clear explanation work together. “Always be prepared to make a defense to anyone who calls you to account for the hope that is in you; yet do it with gentleness and reverence” (1 Peter 3:15).
Mention the new evangelization, called for by John Paul II.
quiz: All the baptized are called to…|Rule|Rest|Evangelize|Hide|2|CCC 905.
Evangelization is…|Shaming|Debating|Winning|Sharing the Good News|3|CCC 853.
The mission is rooted in…|Money|Culture|Politics|Christ’s command|3|Matthew 28:19.
lessons.life: Share your faith in one concrete way.
lessons.saint: Charles Lwanga and the Ugandan martyrs: young converts who chose Christ over a king.
misc: “Evangelization is only for missionaries.”
“Evangelization means arguing people into the Church.”
lessons.mem: “Always be prepared to make a defense to anyone who calls you to account for the hope that is in you.” (1 Peter 3:15)
lessons.hook: Ask: “If someone asked why you believe, what would you say in 30 seconds?” Then read Matthew 28:19–20 and 1 Peter 3:15.
lessons.assess: Ask students to state their testimony and one concrete witness step.

script.open: Hold up a phone with a social media feed. Say, “Everyone shares what they love. What is the best way to share faith so that people hear it and do not just scroll past?” Take suggestions.
teach: Read Matthew 28:18-20. Say: “‘All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me. Go therefore and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, teaching them to observe all that I have commanded you; and lo, I am with you always, to the close of the age.’ The Church exists to evangelize. This is called the Great Commission. Every baptized person shares in it, not only priests and missionaries.”

Say: “Pope Paul VI wrote, ‘The Church exists in order to evangelize.’ Pope Francis called all to be ‘missionary disciples.’ Evangelization means proclaiming Jesus Christ, by word and example, and inviting others to a relationship with him. It includes witness of life, which comes first: ‘Let your light so shine before men that they may see your good works and give glory to your Father who is in heaven.’ (Matthew 5:16) Then comes proclamation: explaining the faith. Peter said: ‘Always be prepared to make a defense to anyone who calls you to account for the hope that is in you; yet do it with gentleness and reverence.’ (1 Peter 3:15)”

Say: “How can we do this in practice? Live your faith joyfully and consistently. Pray for others. Invite a friend to Mass or a youth event. Be ready to share your own story of what Jesus means to you. Know your faith. Treat everyone with respect, listening before talking. Use social media wisely. Serve others. Don’t be pushy or argue just to win. Most people come to faith through a friend. The Holy Spirit does the converting; we are the instruments. And evangelization needs courage, as the Ugandan martyrs showed.”
ask: What did Jesus command in Matthew 28? (Go, make disciples, baptize and teach.)
What comes first in evangelization? (Witness of life.)
Who actually converts hearts? (The Holy Spirit.)
practice: In pairs, practice a two-minute “faith story”: one thing Jesus means to me.
Practice responding gently to a friend who says, “Why do you believe?” or “Why go to Mass?”.
Write a short invitation to a friend for a parish event.
Pray for the friend by name.
script.close: Pray: “Lord, make me a missionary disciple.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Invite someone to Mass.”

tryit: Write your own invitation to faith.
Practice it in pairs.
Say what the witness of a life says.
lessons.saintStory:
In the 1880s, the Catholic missionaries known as White Fathers had come to the kingdom of Buganda, in what is now Uganda. A group of young men, pages in the court of King Mwanga II, became Christians. Joseph Mukasa, the head page, asked the king to stop abusing the boys. Mwanga, enraged, had him beheaded in 1885. Charles Lwanga took his place as the leader, and baptized the younger boys that night.
In 1886, the king demanded that the Christian pages renounce their faith. They refused. On June 3, twenty-two Catholic men and boys, the youngest about thirteen, were burned alive at Namugongo. They went singing hymns. Another set of Anglican converts were also martyred.
The martyrs of Uganda were canonized in 1964. The faith grew rapidly after their deaths. Today Uganda is a heartland of African Catholicism.

units.title: Hard questions: faith, science and history
units.eq: Can I trust a Church that has made mistakes?

lessons.title: Genesis, evolution and the big bang
lessons.idea: Faith and science are both ways of seeking truth, so they cannot truly contradict each other. Genesis teaches why the world exists, not how it works.
lessons.question: Does science disprove the Bible?
lessons.activity: Write two columns: the questions science answers and the questions Genesis answers.
teach: The Church teaches that God created everything and that faith and reason cannot contradict (CCC 159). The Church has not defined how God brought about living things; it teaches that the human soul is created directly by God (CCC 366).

Catholics may accept the big bang and evolution. Fr. Georges Lemaître, a Catholic priest, proposed the big bang theory. Pope Pius XII (Humani Generis, 1950) and St John Paul II (1996) said evolution is not opposed to faith.
The Church reads Genesis for its truths about God, creation, the goodness of the world, the dignity of man and the fall (CCC 289, 337, 390), as sacred writers used stories to teach.
Not every Christian reads Genesis this way. Be kind to classmates who see it differently, and teach what the Church teaches.
talk: What questions does science answer best? What questions can it not answer?
Why might someone think faith and science must fight?
What do the first pages of Genesis teach about the world even if they are not a science book?
quiz: Who proposed the big bang theory?|A Catholic priest, Georges Lemaître|Pope Pius IX|Galileo|Charles Darwin|0|He was a Belgian priest and physicist.
What does the Church teach about the human soul?|It is created directly by God|It is not part of the person|It is a product of the brain only|It evolves from animal souls|0|CCC 366.
Faith and science, rightly understood…|Must always be opposed|Never speak of the same world|Are the same thing|Cannot contradict each other|3|CCC 159.
lessons.life: Ask a science teacher what question first made them curious. Pray a psalm of wonder (Psalm 8).
lessons.saint: Albert the Great: a Dominican who studied rocks, plants and animals to know their Maker.
misc: “The Church says you cannot believe in evolution.”
“Science has proved there is no God.”
lessons.mem: “The heavens declare the glory of God, and the firmament proclaims his handiwork.” (Psalm 19:1)
lessons.hook: Ask: “Where did you first hear that you have to choose between faith and science?” Take a few answers, then say that the Church has never taught that.
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain what Genesis 1 teaches and what questions science answers.

script.open: Ask, “Do you think a person can be a scientist and believe in God? Name any you know.” Take answers. Mention Mendel (a monk who founded genetics), Georges Lemaître (priest who proposed the Big Bang) and others.
teach: Say: “Some people think faith and science are enemies. The Church teaches they are not, since truth cannot contradict truth. Pope John Paul II said, ‘Science can purify religion from error and superstition; religion can purify science from idolatry and false absolutes.’ Science asks how and what; faith asks why and who. Science studies the physical world through observation and experiment. Theology studies the meaning of the world as God’s creation and our relation to him. They answer different questions.”

Say: “Genesis 1-2 is not a scientific description. It teaches religious truths: there is one God who made everything out of nothing; creation is good; humans are made in God’s image, male and female; there is a day of rest; and the world has an order. It uses the symbols and structure of its time. The Church allows that the days may not be literal. St. Augustine, over 1,600 years ago, warned against interpreting Genesis in a way that ‘makes a fool’ of Christians in the eyes of knowledgeable non-believers. The Bible tells us how to go to heaven, not how the heavens go (as Galileo quoted).”

Say: “The Big Bang theory, proposed by Fr. Georges Lemaître, a Belgian priest and physicist, in 1927, says the universe began about 13.8 billion years ago. This fits with the idea that the universe has a beginning. Pope Pius XII noted that this fits the idea of creation, though science cannot prove God. On evolution, the Church allows that the human body may have developed through evolutionary processes, but each human soul is created directly by God (Humani Generis, 1950). What the Church rejects is the claim that matter alone explains everything, or that humans are accidents. Faith and science can cooperate, with humility on both sides.”
ask: Can truth contradict truth? (No.)
What does Genesis 1 teach? (God made everything good, humans in his image, a day of rest.)
Who proposed the Big Bang? (Fr. Georges Lemaître, a priest.)
practice: Make two columns: “What science asks” and “What faith asks.”
Fill in questions: How old is the universe? Why is there something rather than nothing? How did life develop? Why are we here?
Mark which belongs to each, and where they overlap.
Write a sentence summarizing the Church’s position.
script.close: Pray Psalm 19:1 or Psalm 8. Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Look up a Catholic scientist.”

tryit: Sort the claims into Scripture’s teaching and science’s questions.
Write what each can and cannot say.
Summarize the Church’s position.
lessons.saintStory:
Albert was born around 1200 in Germany, to a noble family. He studied at Padua, and joined the Dominicans. He taught in Paris and Cologne, where one of his students was Thomas Aquinas. He was a bishop for a short time, and had to travel on foot because the Dominicans had a rule against riding.
Albert was fascinated by the natural world. He observed plants, animals, minerals, stars and weather, and wrote books on them, correcting errors in earlier writings by direct observation. He wrote that the aim of natural science is “not simply to accept what we are told, but to inquire into the causes of natural things.” Because of his wide learning, he was called Doctor Universalis, “Universal Doctor.”
He taught that faith and reason are not at odds, and that studying creation leads to its Creator. He died in 1280. In 1941 he was named patron of natural scientists.

lessons.title: Galileo, the Inquisition and the Crusades
lessons.idea: The Church is holy, but its members are sinners. The Church admits real wrongs and tries to tell the truth about its past.
lessons.question: Can the Church be holy if its people do wrong?
lessons.activity: Write a fair summary of one event from two points of view.
teach: The Church is holy because of Christ and the Holy Spirit, but it is made of sinners, and it is always in need of purification (CCC 823, 827). Jesus said the weeds grow with the wheat until the harvest (Matthew 13).

Galileo was tried in 1633 for teaching that the earth moves; in 1992 St John Paul II said the judges had made a mistake. The story is more complicated than “religion against science”: many church leaders and scientists were Catholics.

The Crusades and the Inquisition included real violence and injustice. On March 12, 2000 St John Paul II asked forgiveness for the sins of the Church’s children, including violence in the service of truth.
Be wary of both myths: “the Church has done nothing wrong” and “the Church has only done wrong.” Look at the sources.
talk: Why is it harder to say sorry for what a group did than for what I did?
What is the difference between the Church’s teaching and the actions of some of its members?
Why does the truth about the past matter?
quiz: In 1992 Pope John Paul II said about Galileo’s trial that…|Galileo was a heretic|The judges made a mistake|Galileo had been right about everything and the Church had never made an error|The Church should never admit errors|1|He recognized the error.
The Church is called holy because…|The pope is sinless|Its members never sin|Its history has no failures|Christ and the Holy Spirit make it holy, though its members are sinners|3|CCC 823, 827.
What did Pope John Paul II do on March 12, 2000?|Closed the Vatican Library|Ended the Inquisition|Asked forgiveness for the sins of the Church’s children|Canceled the Jubilee|2|The Day of Pardon.
lessons.life: Read a short, fair article about one historical event and share one thing you learned.
lessons.saint: Bartolomé de las Casas: a priest who saw the cruelty of conquest and spent his life defending the Indians.
misc: “The Church burned Galileo at the stake.”
“If members of the Church did wrong, the Church cannot be true.”
lessons.mem: “Let both grow together until the harvest.” (Matthew 13:30)
lessons.hook: Ask: “Is it harder to admit a family member’s mistake or your own?” Frame the lesson as honest history from people who love the Church.
lessons.assess: Ask students to describe one event from two points of view and say what the Church has acknowledged.

script.open: Write three claims on the board: ‘The Church burned Galileo.’ ‘The Crusades were pure greed.’ ‘The Inquisition killed millions.’ Invite students to vote true, partly true, or false. Keep the tally for later.
teach: Say: “The Church is holy but her members are sinners. The Church has done much good, but members have also done wrong, and the Church admits it. In the Jubilee Year 2000, Pope John Paul II asked forgiveness for the sins of Catholics in history. We should look at hard questions honestly, and avoid both myths that the Church is all bad and myths that she is all good. Let’s look at three: Galileo, the Inquisition and the Crusades.”

Say: “Galileo (1564-1642) argued for the Copernican view that the earth moves around the sun. He was a devout Catholic. Many Church scholars were open to the idea, but the evidence was incomplete, and some interpreted certain Bible verses literally. In 1633 he was tried by the Roman Inquisition and forced to recant, and spent his last years under house arrest. He was not tortured or burned. The affair was a mistake, which John Paul II acknowledged in 1992. But the Church did not oppose science in general: she founded universities, and many scientists were clerics. The Inquisition began in the 1100s to investigate heresy. The Roman Inquisition was fairer than many secular courts, and used limited punishments. The Spanish Inquisition, under the Crown from 1478, was harsher; it executed perhaps a few thousand people over centuries, far fewer than legend suggests. Even so, it was wrong to punish people for beliefs by force.”

Say: “The Crusades (1095-1291) were military expeditions called by the popes, initially to defend Eastern Christians and to recover Jerusalem, which Muslim armies had conquered, and to protect pilgrims. They were a mix of faith and politics. There were heroic deeds and great sacrifice, but also atrocities, such as the massacre of Jews in the Rhineland and the sack of Jerusalem in 1099, and the sack of Constantinople in 1204 by Western Crusaders, which deeply wounded relations with the East. The Church today does not defend these abuses. Jesus said, ‘Put your sword back.’ History is complex. We should study it honestly, trusting that truth serves the faith.”
ask: Was Galileo tortured? (No; he was tried and put under house arrest.)
What did John Paul II do in 2000? (Asked forgiveness for the sins of Church members.)
Why study history honestly? (Truth serves the faith.)
practice: Prepare cards of claims: “The Church burned Galileo.” “The Crusades were only about greed.” “The Inquisition killed millions.”
Sort them into: true, partly true, false.
Use a short reading or the lesson’s facts as evidence.
Write one sentence: how I would answer a friend who raised this.
script.close: Pray the prayer of forgiveness: “Lord, forgive the sins of your children, and make us one.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Ask an adult what they have heard about one of these.”

tryit: Sort claims into fact, myth and debate.
Check each against the evidence.
Write what the Church admits and what she denies.
lessons.saintStory:
Bartolomé de las Casas was born in Seville around 1484. He went to the Caribbean in 1502 as a settler, and owned a plantation with native laborers under the encomienda system. He was ordained a priest, the first ordained in the New World. In 1514, while preparing a sermon, he read a passage in Sirach: “Like one who kills a son before his father’s eyes is the man who offers sacrifice from the property of the poor.” He was shaken, freed his laborers, and from then on devoted himself to defending the Indians.
He traveled to Spain over a dozen times to petition the king. He wrote A Short Account of the Destruction of the Indies, describing the atrocities. In 1550 he debated in Valladolid with a scholar, Sepúlveda, who argued that native peoples were natural slaves. Las Casas insisted that they were rational human beings with rights.
He became a Dominican and bishop of Chiapas. He died in 1566. His record is not perfect, but he is remembered as a defender of human rights.

lessons.title: Why does a good God allow suffering?
lessons.idea: God does not will evil, yet allows it for a greater good. In Christ he enters suffering and brings life from it.
lessons.question: If God is good, why is there suffering?
lessons.activity: Write a letter to someone who is hurting.
teach: The Catechism asks the question plainly (CCC 309). There is no single answer; the whole of faith is the answer (CCC 309). God is not the author of evil, and he permits it only to bring a greater good (CCC 311–312).
Some suffering comes from human freedom and sin, some from a world still unfinished (CCC 310). Jesus did not explain suffering away. He shared it, died, and rose.
The right first response to someone suffering is love and presence, not an argument. Job’s friends were wrong when they explained too quickly.
Christians are called to relieve suffering (works of mercy) and to unite their own to Christ (CCC 1521).
talk: Have you ever been helped by someone who just stayed beside you?
Why do arguments often fail a hurting person?
What does the cross tell us about God and suffering?
quiz: Does God cause evil?|He has no power over it|He does not know about it|Yes, to teach lessons|No, he permits it for a greater good|3|CCC 311.
In the book of Job, the friends who explain Job’s suffering as punishment are…|Healed|Praised|Rebuked by God|Ignored|2|Job 42:7.
What does the Catechism say is the answer to the problem of evil?|No answer exists|A single short argument|The whole of the Christian faith|Only science|2|CCC 309.
lessons.life: Visit, call or write to someone who is suffering this week.
lessons.saint: Edith Stein: a philosopher and Carmelite who died at Auschwitz.
misc: “God sends suffering to punish us for specific sins.”
“If God loved us, nothing bad would ever happen.”
lessons.mem: “My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness.” (2 Corinthians 12:9)
lessons.hook: Acknowledge that many students have faced pain. Invite quiet before beginning, and give permission to step out.
lessons.assess: Ask students to state what the Church teaches about God and evil and one way to accompany someone who suffers.

script.open: Be quiet for a moment, then say, “This is the hardest question people ask about God: If God is good and all-powerful, why is there suffering? I want to approach it honestly, because it deserves honesty. Is anyone here comfortable saying they have no pain?”
teach: Say: “The problem of evil is real, and the Church does not pretend there is an easy answer. The Catechism says there is no quick answer; ‘only the Christian message as a whole constitutes the answer.’ (CCC 309) Here are parts of the answer. One: God did not make evil. He made the world good, and gave humans and angels free will. Suffering and death entered through the misuse of freedom, in the fall. Love requires freedom; and freedom can be misused. Two: much suffering results from human sin: war, injustice, cruelty. Natural evils like disease and earthquakes are also consequences of a world that is ‘in a state of journeying’ toward perfection, and of the fall.”

Say: “Three: God can bring good from evil, as with Joseph: ‘You meant evil against me; but God meant it for good.’ We do not say that God causes evil, but he permits it, and brings greater good from it. Four, and most important: God did not stay at a distance. Jesus entered into our suffering. He wept, he was hungry, he was betrayed, he was tortured and killed. God knows suffering from inside. On the cross, he took our pain upon himself. Five: suffering is not the final word. The Resurrection shows that death is defeated. In the end, God ‘will wipe away every tear from their eyes, and death shall be no more.’ (Revelation 21:4)”

Say: “The Book of Job asks the question, and God doesn’t explain, but comes to Job and says that his ways are beyond us. Suffering can also be redemptive when united with Christ. Paul said, ‘I rejoice in my sufferings for your sake, and in my flesh I complete what is lacking in Christ’s afflictions.’ (Colossians 1:24) Suffering can draw us closer to God, teach compassion, and purify us. But it is not good in itself, and we must work to relieve it. And we should not hide our pain: the Psalms complain to God. Mother Teresa, Edith Stein and many others found God in the midst of suffering. This does not completely solve the mystery, but it gives hope and strength.”
ask: Did God make evil? (No; he made the world good and gave freedom.)
What did Jesus do about suffering? (He entered into it and died for us.)
What is the final answer? (The Resurrection and God’s promise to wipe away every tear.)
practice: Write the question at the top: “If God is good, why suffering?”
Make a list of the answers: free will, God brings good from evil, Jesus shares our suffering, resurrection, redemptive suffering.
Choose the answer you find most helpful, and write why.
Write a short honest prayer to God about something hard in your life.
script.close: Pray Psalm 13 or 22, or: “Lord, in my pain, be with me.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Be present to someone who is suffering.”

tryit: Sort the answers to suffering.
Mark where Scripture and the Church speak.
Write a prayer from your own pain.
lessons.saintStory:
Edith Stein was born in 1891 in Breslau, Germany, to a devout Jewish family. As a teenager, she became an atheist. She studied philosophy and became a brilliant assistant to the philosopher Edmund Husserl. During World War I she nursed soldiers. After a friend, a philosopher, was killed in the war, she visited his widow, and was struck by the widow’s faith in the cross. Later, one night in 1921, she read the autobiography of Teresa of Avila, and closed it, saying, “This is the truth.” She was baptized on January 1, 1922.
She taught at a Catholic school, then at a college, until the Nazis forced Jews out of teaching positions. In 1933 she entered the Carmelites in Cologne, taking the name Teresa Benedicta of the Cross. In 1938, for her safety, she was moved to a convent in the Netherlands. When the Dutch bishops condemned the persecution of Jews in 1942, the Nazis arrested all Catholic converts of Jewish descent.
She was taken to Auschwitz with her sister Rosa, and died in the gas chamber on August 9, 1942. She was canonized in 1998.

units.title: Justice, truth and contentment
units.eq: How do we love our neighbor in what we have and what we say?

lessons.title: You shall not steal: justice and respect for goods
lessons.idea: The seventh commandment forbids stealing and cheating and asks us to be fair, honest and generous. God gave the earth to everyone, so we share what we have and care for the poor.
lessons.question: What do justice and generosity ask of us?
lessons.activity: Role-play cases: found money, borrowed items, pirated media, unfair work. Decide what justice requires and how to repair harm.
teach: “You shall not steal” protects the goods of others (CCC 2401–2414). Theft, fraud, cheating, unjust wages and pirating are sins. Restitution repairs the wrong (CCC 2412).
The earth’s goods are meant for everyone, so private property has a social purpose (CCC 2402–2406). Giving to the poor is an act of justice (CCC 2446).
We care for creation and animals (CCC 2415–2418). John the Baptist told soldiers and tax collectors to be fair (Luke 3:10–14).
Be mindful that students may face poverty. Never shame.
talk: When is it hard to be honest about money or things?
How do you repair a wrong?
What can we do for people with less?
quiz: Restitution means…|Hiding it|Repairing what was taken|Blaming|Forgetting|1|CCC 2412.
The goods of the earth are meant for…|Everyone|A few|Kings|Nobody|0|CCC 2402.
Cheating on a test is…|Harmless|A form of dishonesty|Smart|Fine|1|CCC 2409.
lessons.life: Return or repay something you owe, and give to someone in need.
lessons.saint: Elizabeth Ann Seton: a widow who lost her fortune and founded the first Catholic parish school in America.
misc: “If it’s not hurting anyone it’s not stealing.”
“Giving to the poor is optional.”
lessons.mem: “Let him who steals steal no longer, but rather let him labor.” (Ephesians 4:28)
lessons.hook: Ask: “Is it stealing if no one notices?” Discuss the case of copying homework or downloading a movie illegally.
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain justice in goods and propose a repair for a case.

script.open: Hold up a library book or a borrowed item. Say, “Whose is this? What do you owe the owner?” Then write on the board the different ways people take things that are not theirs, from small to large.
teach: Read Exodus 20:15. Say: “‘You shall not steal.’ The seventh commandment protects the right to property and requires respect for others’ goods. It is not only about shoplifting. It forbids theft, robbery, fraud, cheating, breaking contracts, unjust wages, bribery, vandalism, and wasting what belongs to others. It also forbids stealing online: pirating music and software, plagiarism, and copying homework. Ephesians 4:28: ‘Let the thief no longer steal, but rather let him labor, doing honest work with his hands, so that he may be able to give to those in need.’”

Say: “The Church teaches that God gave the earth to everyone. Private property is right and good, but it has a ‘universal destination’: goods are for the benefit of all. Those with abundance have a duty to share. We must care for creation and not exploit it. We should work honestly, pay just wages, keep promises, and pay our debts. If we have taken what is not ours, we owe restitution: returning it or its worth. Zacchaeus is the model. In the sacrament of Penance, the priest will ask us to make restitution when we can.”

Say: “Stealing can be subtle. Taking a few minutes of time you are paid for. Not returning a lent item. Cutting corners in work. Not giving a just share to workers. Neglecting the poor: St. John Chrysostom said, ‘Not to enable the poor to share in our goods is to steal from them. The goods we possess are not ours, but theirs.’ Positive virtues: honesty, generosity, justice, simplicity, gratitude. We are stewards of what God gives us. Jesus asked us to give and to lend, expecting nothing in return.”
ask: What does the seventh commandment forbid? (Theft, fraud, cheating, unjust wages, bribery, damage to property.)
What is restitution? (Returning what was taken, or its value.)
What does the universal destination of goods mean? (God gave the earth for the benefit of all.)
practice: Prepare scenarios: finding $20, copying a friend’s essay, keeping an overpaid change, a download without paying, paying a babysitter less than promised.
For each, decide: just or unjust? What virtue or commandment applies? What should you do?
Choose a past action you might need to repair.
Plan a restitution or generous act.
script.close: Pray: “Lord, teach me to be honest and generous.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Return something you borrowed.”

tryit: Sort actions into just and unjust.
Name the commandment and virtue each touches.
Plan one act of restitution or generosity.
lessons.saintStory:
Elizabeth Bayley was born in 1774 in New York City, to a prominent family. She married a wealthy merchant, William Seton, and they had five children. Their business failed, and William fell ill with tuberculosis. They sailed to Italy hoping for a cure. He died there, leaving Elizabeth a widow at twenty-nine, with five children, penniless in a foreign land.
In Italy, she was cared for by Catholic friends, and became attracted by their faith, especially belief in the Real Presence. She returned to New York and entered the Catholic Church in 1805, which cost her friends and income. A priest invited her to open a school in Baltimore, and she started the Sisters of Charity, the first American religious community. In 1810 they moved to Emmitsburg, Maryland, where she began a school for girls, the start of Catholic parish schools in the United States.
She died in 1821, aged forty-six. In 1975 she became the first American-born saint.

lessons.title: You shall not bear false witness: truth and trust
lessons.idea: The eighth commandment asks us to speak the truth in love. Lies, gossip, rash judgment and betraying secrets harm trust. Jesus is the Truth.
lessons.question: Why does truth matter so much?
lessons.activity: Sort statements into truth, gossip, lies, calumny, detraction, rash judgment. Write a short, kind way to say a hard truth.
teach: Jesus is the Truth (John 14:6). We bear witness to him by truthful speech and sometimes at great cost, as martyrs do (CCC 2464–2474).
Sins against truth: lying, perjury, rash judgment, detraction, calumny, flattery (CCC 2475–2487). Reparation includes correcting the record.
Secrets and privacy are to be respected; the seal of Confession is absolute (CCC 2488–2492). Media and social networks call for honesty and charity (CCC 2493–2499).
Truth must be spoken with love: “speaking the truth in love” (Ephesians 4:15).
talk: When is it hard to tell the truth?
What is the difference between gossip and concern?
How do we handle truth online?
quiz: Detraction is…|Revealing someone’s faults without good reason|Singing|Telling a joke|Praising|0|CCC 2477.
Calumny is…|A prayer|Lying to harm a reputation|A feast|A saint|1|CCC 2477.
We should speak the truth…|Quickly|Never|Cruelly|In love|3|Ephesians 4:15.
lessons.life: Choose to speak only what is true and kind for a day, and make amends where you gossiped.
lessons.saint: Polycarp: a bishop who would not lie, even to save his life.
misc: “White lies don’t matter.”
“Truth should be used as a weapon.”
lessons.mem: “Let your yes be yes and your no be no.” (Matthew 5:37)
lessons.hook: Play “telephone” with a short sentence and compare the end. Ask what happens to trust when words change.
lessons.assess: Ask students to define lying, detraction and calumny and give a repair for each.

script.open: Ask, “Have you ever told a small lie to be polite or to avoid trouble? Did it cause any problem? What would the world be like if no one could trust what anyone said?” Take answers.
