teach: Read Exodus 20:16. Say: “‘You shall not bear false witness against your neighbor.’ The eighth commandment protects truth and trust. It originally referred to false testimony in court, but it covers all lying. Jesus is ‘the truth’ (John 14:6), and the devil is the ‘father of lies’ (John 8:44). Lying means speaking a falsehood with the intent to deceive. Lies destroy trust. A lie is always wrong, even a ‘white lie’ to be polite or to avoid trouble. We can be tactful without lying; and we are not obliged to tell everything.”

Say: “Other sins against the eighth commandment: perjury (lying under oath); rash judgment (assuming evil about someone without proof); detraction (revealing someone’s faults without a good reason); calumny (telling lies that harm someone’s reputation); gossip; flattery; boasting; and breaking promises. Online: spreading rumors, posting embarrassing images, fake accounts, and plagiarism. If we have damaged someone’s reputation, we must repair it, as far as possible. Secrets: priests keep the seal of confession; professionals keep confidences. But we do not keep secrets that put someone in danger. We should tell a trusted adult.”

Say: “The positive side: truthfulness, honesty and integrity. ‘Let what you say be simply Yes or No.’ (Matthew 5:37) We give others the benefit of the doubt. We speak the truth in love (Ephesians 4:15). We use media wisely: seeking facts, and not sharing what we cannot verify. And we bear witness to Christ by our words and lives, even at cost. The martyrs are the ultimate witnesses to truth. Polycarp could have told a small lie, but he would not. Trust is built over years and can be lost in a moment.”
ask: What is a lie? (Speaking a falsehood with intent to deceive.)
What is detraction? (Revealing someone’s faults without good reason.)
What is calumny? (Lies that harm someone’s reputation.)
practice: Write statements on cards: “I didn’t do my homework because I was sick,” “I heard she…,” “Nice haircut” (when you dislike it), “I can’t go; I have plans,” “He cheated, but I won’t say.”
Sort into: truthful, a lie, gossip, calumny, tact.
Discuss tricky cases: what honest, kind responses would you give?
Write a personal rule for speech.
script.close: Pray: “Lord, set a guard over my mouth.” (Psalm 141:3.) Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Go one day without gossip.”

tryit: Sort statements into truth, lie, gossip, calumny and white lie.
Say what each does to trust.
Write a rule for your speech.
lessons.saintStory:
Polycarp was bishop of Smyrna (now Izmir, Turkey) and a disciple of the apostle John. He was one of the Apostolic Fathers. Ignatius of Antioch wrote him a letter on his way to martyrdom. Polycarp wrote a letter to the Philippians, and he visited Rome to talk with Pope Anicetus about the date of Easter.
In about the year 155, when Polycarp was an old man, a persecution broke out in Smyrna. He could have escaped, but was arrested. The proconsul urged him to swear by the emperor’s fortune and curse Christ. “Eighty-six years I have served him,” Polycarp said, “and he has done me no wrong. How can I blaspheme my King who saved me?”
He was burned at the stake, and prayed aloud, giving thanks that he had been counted worthy to be numbered among the martyrs. The account of his death is one of the earliest martyrdom accounts, written by his own community.

lessons.title: You shall not covet: freedom of heart
lessons.idea: The ninth and tenth commandments reach into the heart: purity of heart and freedom from envy and greed. Gratitude, generosity and trust in God make us free.
lessons.question: How do we keep a heart free of envy?
lessons.activity: Write a gratitude list of ten things you have. Then draw a “heart garden” with plants that stand for gratitude, generosity and trust.
teach: The ninth commandment protects purity of heart (CCC 2514–2533). Jesus says, “Blessed are the pure in heart” (Matthew 5:8). Purity needs prayer, modesty and discipline of the senses.
The tenth guards against greed and envy (CCC 2534–2557). Envy is sadness at another’s good; it is a capital sin (CCC 2538–2540).
The remedy is gratitude, humility and trust in providence. “Where your treasure is, there will be your heart also” (Matthew 6:21; CCC 2544–2547).
Teach with compassion. Social media can inflame comparison; invite students to notice it.
talk: How can gratitude change how we see things?
What does a pure heart look like?
quiz: Envy is…|Prayer|Joy|Sadness at another’s good|Courage|2|CCC 2539.
The antidote to envy is…|More stuff|Gratitude and generosity|Hiding|Anger|1|CCC 2540.
Blessed are the pure in heart, for they…|See God|Are rich|Win|Sleep|0|Matthew 5:8.
lessons.life: Every night this week write three things you are thankful for and thank a person for a gift.
lessons.saint: Francis of Assisi: a rich young man who gave up everything and found he was free.
misc: “Wanting things is always wrong.”
“Envy is harmless.”
lessons.mem: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God.” (Matthew 5:8)
lessons.hook: Show two bags of candy, one with more. Ask students how they feel when they see the difference. Name envy.
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain the ninth and tenth commandments and a practice that helps.

script.open: Display a fashion ad or a new-phone ad. Ask, “What does this promise? What feeling is it selling?” Take answers and write them down. Say, “Let’s test whether the promise is true.”
teach: Read Exodus 20:17 and Luke 12:15. Say: “‘You shall not covet your neighbor’s house… or anything that is your neighbor’s.’ The tenth commandment goes to the heart. The seventh forbids taking; the tenth forbids even wanting what belongs to another in a way that leads to envy or greed. Jesus said, ‘Take heed, and beware of all covetousness; for a man’s life does not consist in the abundance of his possessions.’ Coveting is the root of many sins. It is a disordered desire that makes us unhappy.”

Say: “Greed is the desire for more and more. Envy is sorrow at another’s good and wanting it for ourselves; it is one of the capital sins. In the Bible, Cain envied Abel, Joseph’s brothers envied him, and Saul envied David. Social media can feed envy, since we see only others’ best moments. The remedy is gratitude, humility and generosity. Detachment from possessions: Jesus said, ‘Blessed are the poor in spirit.’ Paul wrote, ‘I have learned, in whatever state I am, to be content… I can do all things in him who strengthens me.’ (Philippians 4:11-13)”

Say: “Poverty of spirit does not mean we must all be poor. It means we don’t cling to things, we use them with gratitude and share them. Simplicity brings freedom. Francis and Clare showed that. The Church also asks us to guard the heart from impure desires, the ninth commandment. All of these commandments concern the heart: ‘Create in me a clean heart, O God.’ The goal is to desire what is truly good: God himself. Augustine prayed, ‘Our hearts are restless until they rest in you.’ The best remedy for envy is to rejoice in another’s good, and thank God for our own.”
ask: What does the tenth commandment forbid? (Envy and greed; disordered desire for others’ goods.)
What is the remedy for envy? (Gratitude, humility, rejoicing in others’ good.)
What does ‘poor in spirit’ mean? (Not clinging to possessions; trusting God.)
practice: Make two lists: things you want, and things you need.
Beside each “want,” ask: Where did this want come from (an ad, a friend, a post)?
Choose one thing you can give away or give up, and a person who needs it.
Write three things you are grateful for.
script.close: Pray the Prayer of Saint Francis: “Lord, make me an instrument of your peace.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Give away something this week.”

tryit: Make a list of what you want and what you need.
Find the root of each want.
Choose one thing to give away.
lessons.saintStory:
Francis was born around 1181 in Assisi, the son of a wealthy cloth merchant. He was charming, fun-loving and wanted to be a knight. After being captured in a war and falling ill, he began to wonder what his life was for. One day, he met a leper on the road, and, though revolted, got down from his horse and kissed his hand. Soon after, in the ruined chapel of San Damiano, he heard the crucifix say, “Francis, repair my house.”
He took cloth from his father’s shop and sold it to repair the chapel. His angry father took him to the bishop of Assisi. Francis took off his clothes, handed them to his father, and said, “Until now I have called you my father on earth; now I can say freely, ‘Our Father who art in heaven.’” He chose a life of poverty, preaching and serving the poor.
Others joined him, and the Franciscans were founded. Francis sang about “Brother Sun and Sister Moon.” He died in 1226, naked on the ground, at peace.
